#817. Whoopi Goldberg Details Bond With "Irreplaceable" Patrick Stewart

Whoopi Goldberg honored Sir Patrick Stewart after sharing decades of friendship with her Star Trek: The Next Generation costar before his Oct. 28 death at 86 years old.

Whoopi Goldberg's friendship with Patrick Stewart meant the world—and beyond—to her.

In remembering the Star Trek: The Next Generation alum after his Oct. 28 death following a brief battle with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia, Goldberg expressed how precious her decades-long friendship with the late 86-year-old was.

"We lost a wonderful actor and a great human being this weekend. My friend, Sir Patrick Stewart, he passed away." Goldberg—who played Guinan to his Captain Jean-Luc Picard—remarked on The View Nov. 2. "He is, in a word, irreplaceable, really."

And their bond—which began in the '80s when they costarred in the sci-fi series—was one that withstood the test of time. As the 70-year-old explained, "We went way back, and I adored him."

In addition to their personal relationship, the Ghost actress recognized Stewart's incomparable legacy in the public eye as photos from his iconic career flashed on screen, including a shot of his character Professor Charles Xavier in X-Men.

"As a performer, he could do everything," Goldberg continued. "He could do drama, science fiction, comedy, and of course Shakespeare."

As such, she treasured getting to work alongside the famed thespian again in 2022 after Stewart invited her to reprise her role in Star Trek: Picard during a visit to the morning show. Goldberg said the "amazing" memory makes her "just giggle all over the place."

"Star Trek remains one of the great events in my life," she explained of her time playing his onscreen confidante. "I'll miss him dearly, but he's up with a lot of great people, so I know he's running around having fun."

The comedian first celebrated her late friend's life by sharing a photo of their Star Trek characters as action figures, captioned, "See you on the next holodeck @sirpatstew RIP."

And Goldberg is in good company when it comes to appreciating Stewart's one-of-a-kind humor and kindness. Boldly go and read more moving remembrances…

"We first met as ambitious young actors with the Royal Shakespeare Company half a century ago but we weren’t in the same productions. My first strong memory was a few years later, meeting him in the street in central London when he told me about an offer to take over a leading part in Star Trek. 'But Patrick think of your stage career in the UK. Do you really want to risk—getting lost in Hollywood for years and years?' Well, he took the risk and thank goodness for us all that he did for not just his devoted Trekkies but film and theatre audiences, who marvelled at his using international celebrity to star in a string of cinema successes (X-Men of course) and in great classical plays by Shakespeare, Ibsen, Arthur Miller, Peter Shaffer, Pinter and Beckett at Stratford-upon-Avon, in London’s West End and on Broadway."

"We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today. And, in my book, a tremendous friend and man. I learned so much from him. I will miss you, Patrick Stewart, all of my days."

"Patrick was one of those icons who we somehow all took for granted would always be with us. I grew up as a fan, and was later gifted the privilege of becoming a colleague and friend, working with him for many years on American Dad!, Family Guy, and Ted. He was that rare actor who could take any bit of dialogue and elevate it, making a good writer sound great, and a great writer sound masterful. He was also as humble as they come. I remember exchanging emails with him a number of years ago when he was beginning day 1 of a new film. He commented to me that he always walked onto a new set feeling like the biggest novice there. My stunned reaction was the same as anyone’s would be. I said, 'Patrick, if you feel that way, the rest of us are screwed.' We have lost a legendary actor today, and for many of us, a good friend. He will be deeply missed by the entire planet."

"What a heartbreaking week it has been. Sir Patrick Stewart was a friend, a colleague, and a magnificent actor. From the stage to the bridge of the Enterprise, he brought intelligence, grace, and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did. Captain Picard stood for the best of us, and so did the man who played him. I was filled with affection and admiration for him and his work."

"I feel so grateful to have known him for the last 25 years and to have been in his orbit for the last 25 years, both as a fellow 'mutant' and as a fellow member of Starfleet. He was positively delicious, hilarious, naughty, incredible sense of humor, and that booming voice of his that always spoke to the very back of the room—as every classically trained Shakespearean great needs to master—has always been an Inspiration. I'm gonna send my condolences to his family, and I'll miss my friend dearly. Rest in peace, Patrick."

"My friend, we shared some memorable times…from the deserts of Arrakis to the mysterious jungles of Thailand and onto the New York stage. I already miss you. You will always be my Gurney Halleck and I, your young pup."

"Patrick Stewart is a legend. His acting talent was not only innate but built from his professionalism, his dedication to craft, his enthusiasm, his generosity, his gentlemanly way of being. He was mischievous and game, always made me laugh and always made a day better. He leaves a treasure trove of work behind and I’m so grateful he came to play w me on Charlie’s Angels. Rest peacefully Patrick. Sending love."

"Patrick Stewart was one of the greats, not just because of his extraordinary talent, but because of the man he was. It was a privilege to work alongside him and an even greater pleasure to know him personally. He was loved by all and will be deeply missed. My heart goes out to his family and loved ones."

"Dearest Patrick. Such sad news and a huge loss for us all. RIP."

"PStew, lover of fresh produce and classic american western songs. a man who even at 80 could recite every work of shakespear[e] he’s ever done. a man who once handed me his drink so he could do five pull ups on the branch of a tree. a man with so much love and respect for his craft and fellow artists. one of the first people in this business to take a chance on me. so grateful to have witnessed his greatness on and off the stage and screen. rest in peace."

"Thank you, Pstew, for being my friend, for being so kind and generous with your heart, for being so funny and vulnerable, and for being so talented and inspiring. Getting cast as Raffi on Star Trek Picard has been a gift that keeps on giving, but the best part was meeting YOU, working with you, and becoming your friend. I am, and always will be, grateful for this amazing experience and adventure we shared. I love you and will miss you, my dear sweet friend. The world lost a great one today... Rest now, Captain, my captain."

"Ouch. This one hurts. Rest well, Patrick."

"He was such a kind, genuine, funny, unique, caring and charming man. I remember his endless jokes, nurturing nature and colourful reading glasses. Every single day spent working by his side was an honour and a privilege I can’t quite believe I had. He was a walking master of his craft, and of life. One of the greatest of our time, on stage and on screen. I have always looked up to him, and always will. As an actor and as a man. He had a wonderful way of wrapping every ancient lesson he imparted in wonder, fun and excitement. I will always remember his warmth and the respect he showed to everyone around him. I will forever hold those months we spent together close to my heart, and will always think of him as a pivotal part of how I view the world around me. So rest in peace, you giant, you legend amongst men. The beautiful work, humanity and kindness you leave behind will live on forever."

"Fans across the world mourn the passing of a true and irreplaceable legend. As Captain Jean-Luc Picard, Patrick Stewart took the starship Enterprise to places it had never gone before, and he inspired a whole next generation of star-gazers who looked longingly ahead to a brighter future for all humanity. Our hearts are heavy, indeed. Rest in the heavens, Captain."

#816. Tenerife player in intensive care with injury

Tenerife won promotion back to Spain's Segunda Division in May 2026

Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel is in a stable condition in intensive care after suffering a serious injury during a Spanish second division match on Monday.

The 30-year-old suffered injuries in the region of his head and chest in added time of Tenerife's home fixture against Andorra, following a collision with visiting goalkeeper Jesus Owono.

Spanish media, including Marca, external, reported De Miguel suffered a cardiac arrest in the ambulance and was resuscitated by paramedics on the way to hospital.

A statement from Tenerife said the Madrid-born De Miguel was admitted to the University Hospital of Nuestra Senora de Candelaria and was "stable despite the severity of his condition".

Tenerife and Andorra were tied 2-2 and seven minutes into stoppage time when the incident occurred.

Owono had run towards the centre circle to clear a long ball when his knee appeared to collide with De Miguel.

De Miguel lay motionless on the pitch as medical staff treated him before he was taken by ambulance from Tenerife's Estadio Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez to hospital.

Players from both teams were visibly distressed by the incident, with a number of De Miguel's team-mates in tears.

The referee showed Owono a straight red card before abandoning the match.

A statement from Andorra said: "We want to send all our strength and best wishes to Jesus de Miguel after the serious incident suffered during today's match.

"We hope he recovers soon. A very strong hug to the player, his family and Tenerife."

#815. Arsenal have everything they need to repeat as Premier League champions | Jonathan Wilson

Sunday’s win at Liverpool showed the Gunners are deeper, more experienced, and are playing against a weaker class of contenders than last season

Arsenal are three points clear at the top of the Premier League table. But given the team in second are Manchester City, who are likely to be facing at the very least a major points deduction, perhaps more significant is that they are five clear of Brighton in third. The season of domination that many anticipated from the champions appears to be coming to pass.

Liverpool challenged them on Sunday. There was a 20-minute spell before half-time when they swarmed all over Arsenal, and Anfield felt at least like it did in the golden years of Jürgen Klopp, when it buzzed with an energy that could overwhelm visitors. But Arsenal got through that, reset at half-time, and navigated the second half with relative comfort. For the second league game running, they denied Liverpool a shot on target.

If there is a lesson, it is that Liverpool, like Brighton, demonstrated that a very aggressive press can unsettle Arsenal. But then, a very aggressive press can unsettle anybody. In Arsenal’s loss at Brighton, Pascal Gross and Charalampos Kostoulas took difficult opportunities; at Anfield Liverpool were denied what should surely have been a penalty when Jurriën Timber tugged Alexander Isak’s shirt – another bad moment for VAR, in that the no-call essentially mandated players to go down and highlight contact. Later, Alexis Mac Allister put a free header over. That was the difference, and this Arsenal team will not give opponents many chances. They are good at closing games out. Ezri Konsa in particular was outstanding on Sunday.

They also have a strong bench. The policy has been to make the squad deeper rather than adding the very highest quality – which is why the links with Vinícius Júnior over the summer were so unexpected. That has frustrated some, but it has been successful. Arsenal on Sunday could bring on Myles Lewis-Skelly, Piero Hincapié, Viktor Gyökeres and Mikel Merino to protect their lead with very little diminution of quality. But it’s not just on a man-to-man level that Liverpool’s options suffer by comparison; their changes upset the balance. They never really had control of the game once Dominik Szoboszlai had come on for Trey Nyoni.

It’s been a recurring feature of this season that Arsenal turn half-time draws into full-time wins – it’s already happened seven times. Winning individual games, though, is only part of it; a deeper squad means there can be more rotation, which should help prevent fatigue as the season goes on, as well as providing additional cover when injuries do occur. That said, their depth was not sufficient to get them past Fleetwood in the Carabao Cup last week, although they will face few games in conditions as challenging as those on the Lancashire coast.

There are still three-quarters of the season to go, and Arsenal were in a similarly commanding position at this stage last season, four points clear of second-placed Bournemouth after nine games. The expectation then was for a procession that didn’t materialise and looked, amid a spring wobble, to have gone awry. Then as now the feeling was not merely that Arsenal were very good, but that none of their rivals looked especially threatening.

But this season they have the memory of winning the title; the insecurity of three successive second-place finishes should be lessened. There is a resilience to them that has already brought a first win at Anfield since 2012 and a victory at Nottingham Forest after successive goalless draws at the City Ground. They’re picking up points at grounds where they’ve stumbled.

Last season, City were more resilient than had been anticipated. It may be a different story this time, and not just because of the potential for a savage points deduction. After seven straight wins they have lost successive league games to Aston Villa and Brighton, but the vulnerabilities that have been exposed had been apparent earlier in the season: a high defensive line that can be exploited. Liverpool are starting to coalesce under Andoni Iraola but they haven’t clicked quite yet and are, anyway, nine points adrift. Chelsea are a point better off but still a work in progress. Brighton have probably been the best other side, but they don’t have the depth to be considered a title challenger.

Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.

Sunday made clear what was already widely suspected: Arsenal are the best team in the league by some margin. It’s not just their depth, their cohesion and the wide variety of situations from which they can score goals, it’s that they now have belief and are picking up points at places where they have often failed in the past. And if they do build up a substantial lead by Easter, that could be hugely beneficial to their European challenge, which remains the one unconquered frontier.

#814. US sanctions target Iran's rail sector as Tehran shifts cargo from sea routes to overland corridors

As US sanctions expand to Iran's rail sector, Tehran is relying more heavily on overland links with China and Central Asia. But capacity constraints, delays and costs limit rail's ability to replace maritime trade.

The United States has opened another front in its economic pressure campaign against Iran, this time targeting the railways Tehran increasingly relies on as maritime trade becomes more difficult.

On October 1, the US Treasury sanctioned three Iranian railway companies alongside seven automakers and five foreign suppliers of automotive parts as part of its Operation Economic Outcast.

Washington says Iran's rail and automotive industries provide revenue and logistical capacity to the state and are connected to networks involving the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

The timing of the move is significant. Since the US maritime blockade sharply restricted Iran's southern trade routes, Tehran has tried to move more goods through its land borders and railway connections with China, Central Asia, Russia and Turkey.

Rail transport has become more important just as Washington decided to target it.

Shahriar Naghizadeh, director general for foreign trade at Iran's railway authority, was quoted by the semi-official Mehr news agency as saying that the country has around 15,000 kilometers (9,300 miles) of main and secondary railway lines, more than 35,000 wagons and nearly 500 diesel locomotives.

The network carried around 44 million tons of freight in the Iranian year ending in March 2026, up from about 40 million tons the previous year, according to Naghizadeh. And authorities are targeting 54 million tons this year.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Iran is linked to neighboring markets through 13 rail crossings, providing overland access to Turkey, Azerbaijan, Afghanistan, Pakistan and onward routes to Central Asia and China via Turkmenistan.

The new US sanctions raise questions about how foreign railway operators, freight forwarders, banks and insurers will continue dealing with Iranian rail companies.

Bloomberg reported in May that freight trains traveling from the Chinese city of Xi'an to Tehran had increased from around one per week before the US blockade to roughly one every three or four days.

In September, a train left China carrying automotive parts, consumer goods and other cargo. It ran through Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan before entering Iran at Sarakhs with an expected transit time of 14 to 16 days.

For Iran, such services offer a route to Chinese suppliers that avoids the area around the Strait of Hormuz. But advertised transit times do not necessarily reflect what an importer experiences.

A Chinese freight company told DW that actual delivery times can stretch far beyond advertised schedules because of border inspections, customs procedures and train availability.

It estimated that rail transit along the main route from western China to Tehran would take 50-60 days under current conditions. Road transport along a similar route is around 22 to 25 days.

The gap between a scheduled 14-day transit time and commercial estimates of up to 60 days highlights one of the central challenges facing Iran.

Customs inspections, gauge changes, payment problems and sanctions can all be another potential point of delay.

Increasing the number of trains also requires more locomotives, wagons and cooperation from several transit countries.

Alireza Salavati, managing director of London-based Middle East Analytica, said rail is increasingly useful for Iran but should not be mistaken as a replacement for maritime trade.

"A workable overland route now links China and Iran, but I would not call it a replacement for sea freight," he told DW.

Under normal conditions, ships can move far larger quantities at lower unit costs. Rail becomes more attractive for goods where speed and continuity matter more than the cheapest transport.

That includes automotive components, machinery, electronics and industrial inputs, whose absence can stop an entire production line.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Salavati argues that the effect on companies cannot be measured only in freight charges.

For a manufacturer importing $1 million (€890,000) worth of inputs every 30 days, a 30-day journey means roughly a million dollars of inventory may be tied up in transit.

Cutting the journey to 15 days could reduce that amount significantly, depending on payment arrangements. The reverse can be much more damaging.

If input costs rise while delivery times stretch from 30 to 45 days, companies need more working capital simply to maintain the same production flow, the expert explained, pointing out that a factory can have customers and orders but still have to reduce production because too much cash is trapped in goods that have not arrived.

"Reliability matters as much as speed," Salavati said. "A 15-day train is little use if the container waits a week to depart, or if the bank or insurer will not touch it."

The new US sanctions add another source of uncertainty to that calculation.

Optimizing its railway use would give Iran more options than having to rely on southern ports alone, but the overall scale remains limited.

Washington's sanction strategy is designed to isolate Iran by closing maritime, financial, aviation and now railway channels.

Still, Salavati argues that the same pressure may accelerate Iran's integration with alternative networks.

"Washington's efforts to isolate Iran may also be pushing it deeper than at any point in recent years into China's economic orbit and closer to Russia's wartime strategic system," he said.

That does not mean China or Russia can make up for the economic cost of US pressure, since Iranian importers still need insurers, banks and customers able to absorb higher prices.

Container trains can only carry a fraction of what a large cargo vessel can transport, so for now, rail provides Iran with a limited alternative trade channel.

Its wider success depends on better financing and becoming more reliable — but even then it is not a wholesale substitute for sea freight.

#813. Country Star Maggie Rose Brings a Rock 'n' Roll Edge to Coastal Style

Statement coats, vintage-inspired denim, cheeky graphic tees and cozy knitwear give Maggie Rose’s curated collection a laid-back California feel with a cool-girl edge.

Country star Maggie Rose has teamed up with Carve Designs on a curated collection that feels like a vintage rocker found her way to the California coast. Think statement outerwear, cool girl denim, playful T-shirts, and cozy knitwear with an easygoing, Gold Coast feel.

Launched November 2, the collection brings together Maggie’s personal style and the California-based brand’s laid-back aesthetic. Its versatile pieces are made for the many roles women move between every day, whether that means heading onstage or spending time with family.

“When I feel comfortable, I feel confident. And when I feel confident, I can be fully present,” Maggie says about the collaboration. “That’s how I feel in every piece of this collection. Whether I’m performing in front of thousands of people or reading bedtime stories to Graham, I just want to feel beautiful, comfortable, and completely like myself.”

With their shared love of nature, life and a little rock-and-roll edge, Rose and Carve Designs make a perfect pairing.

“This partnership felt so natural because Carve is a women-run brand that understands that women are multi-faceted, dynamic and complex beings,” she said. “We’re artists, moms, businesswomen, athletes and travelers—We wear a lot of hats…and pants and dresses! I love that Carve celebrates all of those different sides of who we are, instead of asking us to choose just one.”

From vintage-inspired silhouettes to statement prints and graphics, the fun capsule makes it easy to bring a little rock-and-roll attitude to everyday dressing—without losing that polished, retro California spirit.

#812. Hibs toast win over Hearts - but will they kick on before cup final?

Hibs players joined their fans in a stirring rendition of Sunshine On Leith

Such were Marink Reedijk's wishes, shared in an official Hibernian video, external from the dressing room following their historic Hampden beating of Heart of Midlothian in the Scottish League Cup semi-final.

If the Hibs head coach ventured into Leith on Sunday night he would not have been short of offers for both, as he has instantly scribbled his name into the history books.

His wait for a first win in charge ended at game five. As player of the match Joe Newell said afterwards: "I would have taken four losses if this was the way it clicked."

There was a wee wait for Reedjik to break his Hibs duck, but that is nothing compared to the agony Hibs supporters had endured since 2006 when travelling across the M8 to face their city rivals at the national stadium.

Four visits, four endings with jubilant Jambos. Until now.

The sights and sounds of Sunshine on Leith being belted from the east end of the national stadium will take some time to shift, for this is a win Hibs must savour.

Self-professed "ice king" Reedijk revelled in the iconic anthem but admitted it is his responsibility to make "rational decisions" and so remove himself from the "lovely atmosphere".

He will know he and his players must make this moment the launchpad as they attempt to lift off the bottom of the Scottish Premiership.

After he has enjoyed the tunes and pints, of course.

Hibs edge Hearts in thrilling derby to reach League Cup final

Giant curiosity Hibs finally liberated from the sucker punch

McInnes demands more after delivering Rangers' trophy chance

Who could have thought it would have played out this way?

On the eve of their big trip west, Hibs had slipped - again - to the foot of the league table after Kilmarnock picked up a point at home to the 10 men of St Johnstone.

A shocking place for this squad to be, but it was - temporarily - rendered meaningless 24 hours later.

Given their turbulent start to the season - missing out on Europe, failing to win at home and changing managers - being backed by 19,000 supporters was something in itself.

Finally, they were rewarded. Those who travelled to Warsaw last year to lose out on goal difference to Legia and returned from Gent in August with an abundance of hope only to have it dashed at Easter Road, had their moment of joy. And they rightly milked it.

When Jordi Altena's deep free-kick in the 93rd minute ended in goalkeeper Raphael Sallinger's hands, the roar from the other end of Hampden shook the steps on which Hearts supporters were already hovering in search of a swift exit.

Those clad in maroon - all 23,000 of them present and the many others in Gorgie - are surely the only beings unmoved by the inimitable Sunshine on Leith.

Newell had his hands on his head. Boyhood Hibee Jason Kerr was holding back the tears. Nicky Cadden was singing from chest. Arm in arm, Hibs were a unit, as they were from the minute they conceded.

"I love these kind of things" - Marink Reedijk on spine-tingling rendition of Sunshine on Leith

At that point, Newell - who proceeded to pull the strings - was full of fear.

A simple but strong header from Claudio Braga, before many supporters had even taken to their seats, brought concern.

Could a repeat of that unforgettable afternoon - Hibs supporters aren't allowed to forget it - 14 years ago, when Hearts fired five past them in the Scottish Cup final, be on the cards?

"The game plan was out the window," midfielder Newell said. "It's not ideal, is it?

"You go to bed [on Saturday night] thinking of all the scenarios and the way you dream and imagine the game is going to go and then, after two minutes, they score.

"But I think, if anything, it shows how good the character is and kind of emphasises it was even more of a special performance, not just the win."

Which is, surely, what Reedijk and his team will take out of this the most. Any team can win a cup game, but not any team can show the grit, determination and depth Hibs did in setting up a final against Rangers next month.

The showpiece is six weeks away. Few clubs more than Hibs know how much can change in that time frame.

They have as many league games in that period, with the last - of course - being a dress rehearsal of the final as they welcome Derek McInnes' side to Easter Road.

While those in green and white admitted post-match it would be difficult not to think of their return to Hampden - when they will be aiming for the club's first silverware since beating the Ibrox side in the 2016 Scottish Cup final - they know they need to arrest their current league form.

With just two wins in 11 games, they have a trip to struggling Aberdeen - who lost in Saturday's semi-final - on Saturday before welcoming both Dundee clubs to the capital.

Trips to Motherwell and Kilmarnock respectively follow before that meeting with the Light Blues as they search for some much-needed points.

The hope is this performance and result will kick-start their quest to climb the table.

"It's huge," 33-year-old Newell added. "You kind of forget that there's a cup final after that, do you know what I mean?

"You feel like you want to say, that's it done because it felt massive. These games are always huge no matter where they are, but we have to kick on now.

"We have to use it and hopefully it gives all the boys confidence, because it should do. We were outstanding."

Do that, and repeat this result against Rangers on 13 December, and Reedijk and co will never be left wanting for music and beer in Leith ever again.

#811. Revisiting the Superclásico: a story of death, violence, colour and family

Attending Boca v River in the week I turned 60 made me recall a lifetime of experiences at the fixture

Ever since the Observer Sport Monthly published a list of 50 sporting things you must do before you die with Watch Boca Juniors Play River Plate in Buenos Aires at No 1 in 2004, the biggest super derby in Argentina has been firmly positioned in the global imagination; its reputation for colour, passion and uncontainable emotion acquiring an almost glamorous sheen. The thump and thud of the coordinated chants, the shiny ticker-tape amid flare smoke matching the teams’ strips, the bounce of the concrete as tens of thousands jump in unison, mounted police surrounding the stadium, avalanche stoppers set alight, rockets aimed at players; blood and fire.

Things have changed, though, and Sunday at La Bombonera (Boca’s stadium known as the Chocolate Box) was quite a different spectacle. Since 2013 football matches in Argentina have been played without visiting fans, so for starters the colour palette has been greatly reduced. The absence of the opposing tribe has been welcomed by many, making the experience of going to a football match more family-friendly and increasing ticket availability for club members.

As we shared a choripán in a corner grill before the game, the Argentinian journalist Ezequiel Fernández Moores recalls the first Superclásico without away fans, at the Monumental in 2013. As Boca’s Emmanuel Gigliotti scored to give the away team the lead, in the press area Moores heard the beginning “G” of someone ready to shout the goal with glee, suddenly realising “non-home joy had to be repressed”.

Over the years the absence of away fans has been mirrored in an absence of away press. Now the journalists sit at their desks along the same height as the middle tier of the traditional home end, where the heart of the hardcore organised gang known as La Doce leads the rhythm section, creating a sense of continuum, with hacks clad in Boca strips cursing and cheering along with the crowd.

Rain had been forecast for Sunday so Boca distributed blue and yellow umbrellas which opened in sync and matched the colour of the smoke from the fireworks organised by the club.

The pyrotechnics used to be smuggled in by La Doce, who would also orchestrate the release of blue and golden balloons at the exact time the players emerged from the tunnel. When I went to pick up my accreditation, the head press officer announced to no one in particular that this “Señora” (meaning me) had once interviewed José Barritta. A young man holding a newborn baby and a couple of kids who looked barely out of school just stared. “The day of the Ambush,” I stated by way of explanation.

Barritta was the infamous leader of La Doce decades ago and in 1994 I did indeed spend the afternoon with him to write a colour piece about the Superclásico from the “middle tray” (the terraces are tiered in three balconies and the middle one is the centre of operations). It was an afternoon that would end in tragedy with two River Plate fans shot dead after the game. Disgustingly, graffiti emerged nearby soon afterwards reading “River 2 Boca 2”, equating two young lives to the two goals River had scored against Boca securing their victory.

My feature was shelved and instead I became a witness to the fact that Barritta had not been involved, my work published in a human rights journal, and my interest in football-related violence swiftly losing the wide-eyed fascination.

Death at the Superclásico was not something new, even then. In 1968, 71 fans – mostly Boca – were crushed when one of the exit gates for away supporters didn’t fully open. Known as the incident of Puerta 12, much of what actually happened remains unknown, but El Gráfico reported the following year’s game saw members of both Boca and River fans chant together against the police. In those days both gangs were friendly, with then-Boca gang leader Quique, who ran a grill opposite the stadium, buying meat from River gang leader “El Tano Mingo”, who was a butcher. They would often join forces and combat against other club gangs well into the mid-1970s when the leaderships changed. Barritta took the helm of La Doce in 1981, by which time the rupture was total.

In 2018 Boca and River met in the Libertadores final, South America’s version of the Champions League, and the Argentina president, Mauricio Macri, thought it might be fun to show the world what a colourful spectacle the Superclásico might be, so away fans were allowed back to the stadium in a one-off experiment. After the Boca bus was attacked with stones and crowd control fell apart around the inner ring surrounding the River stadium, fans were kept under strict orders to remain in place for close to five hours while the powers that be discussed options. The match was cancelled and outrageously moved to Madrid, where one could argue the soul of the Superclásico has remained, if it hadn’t been sucked out already.

Sunday’s game was not a fixture of the calibre of a Libertadores final. In fact, the strangeness of the current system in Argentina means it was almost inconsequential for either cup or league, although a total points system known as the Argentina Table has implied that Boca’s underwhelming 1-0 victory against a River side down to nine men by the end means Boca have a place in next year’s Libertadores.

“I’ve seen better Superclásicos,” said the radio commentator Victor Hugo Morales in his tiny cabin at the stadium. He was commemorating 60 years to the day of his very first radio commentary, back in Uruguay in 1966. I went along to exchange greetings, as I was commemorating 60 years to the day of being alive. “But I’ve also seen worse,” he added.

That must be debatable, though I’ve probably not seen as many as him. The derby doesn’t always offer the best football, often too embroiled in the hype and the media frenzy surrounding it, and the massive banners and flags obscuring the view for most of the pitch. I started going to the Bombonera with my cousins as a teenager, and the most poignant memory of the fixture was taking my 10-year-old brother along without telling my dad. In those days, women and children got in for free. On Sunday, tickets were going for half a million pesos (£240).

I remember grabbing the little boy by the waist of his trousers as I saw him flying above a sea of sweaty men, as I heard someone shout: “Careful you lot, there’s a ‘Señora’ here!” I was 20. I felt perfectly safe, but I couldn’t convey that to my furious father, who I don’t think I’d ever seen so angry, before or since.

Years later, when TV rights took possession of the industry and football became pay-per-view, my dad was one of the early adopters of a codified system which enabled live watching. I suggested our dear family friend Klaus, a River fan, desperate to watch the Superclásico, join my brothers and cousins atDad’s. Klaus didn’t reveal his allegiance and sat quietly in grief while the assorted Boca fiends jumped about in joy when they won. The anecdote is remembered fondly to this day in my family but for him it was a particularly unpleasant experience.

Maybe new generations will be better at bridging the cultural crack. Streamer Davo, the face of new sports media, was nonchalant before the game. “Don’t give me all this Superclásico nonsense. For me, nothing changes if River beats us this game. I’m focused on the Argentina Cup, on the South American final … this is just another match.”

Also seemingly oblivious to the hyped-up frenzied vitriol, my own son had suggested we go to the game together. He, a River fan, however, could not in any realistic sense attend. I’d love to go to a Superclásico with my son, neither one of us banned by the other’s tribe. Maybe one day.

#810. See Hoda Kotb & Ex Joel Schiffman's Halloween Reunion With Daughters

Hoda Kotb and her ex-fiancé Joel Schiffman wore matching deviled eggs costumes while celebrating Halloween with their daughters Haley, 9, and Hope, 7.

Hoda Kotb and her ex-fiancé Joel Schiffman had an egg-cellent Halloween together.

The former couple reunited to spend the spooky holiday with their daughters Haley, 9, and Hope, 7, wearing matching deviled eggs costumes as they went trick-or-treating as a family.

In a video posted to Kotb's Instagram Oct. 31, the Today alum and Schiffman donned red devil horns and large cutouts of an egg, while their kids dressed as Poppy and Viva from the Trolls movies.

Posing in front of her home, Kotb wrote in the caption, "Happy halloween."

And this wasn't the first time the 62-year-old reunited with Schiffman, 68, to celebrate a special occasion with Haley and Hope. In September, the two were on hand to send their girls off to their first day of school.

"It’s here," Kotb captioned Instagram photos of the family drop-off. "4th and 2nd grade! Whaaaatttt?"

And though it's been four years since the former morning show host ended her engagement to Schiffman, her bond with the financier will always remain strong.

“I loved Joel then, and I love Joel now,” Kotb said on Today last year. “I just had to remind myself that it was a different kind of love.”

In fact, she believes their current dynamic is "the right relationship for us to have."

“We will co-parent in a beautiful way,” Kotb shared, “but I also think our ‘us’ is more of a, like, we’re dear friends now. And that’s beautiful, and it’s enjoyable and it feels right."

That's also because she and Schiffman are "honest" about their co-parenting relationship.

“Kids catch pretending. They know that Joel and I care so much for each other, and they also know that we love them dearly," Kotb added. “I really adore Joel, and they know it. I’m not pretending, I’m not faking it. So, once they see that, they go, ‘Ah, OK. This is good. This is good for us.’”

#808. Newcastle unrest grows as Barry and Everton give Jaissle another headache

Jack Grealish will do well to get back into the Everton starting lineup when he returns to the squad – as David Moyes’s side are doing just fine without him.

Newcastle were condemned to a second defeat in five days by Moyes’s young team, with a second-half goal from Thierno Barry giving Everton victory against 10 men at St James’ Park after the substitute Jacob Ramsey’s late red card.

And there are still more questions than answers about Matthias Jaissle’s new-look side following a summer of transition at the club, and supporters again voiced their disapproval at the end of the game.

Moyes was reluctant to talk about Grealish’s situation, stating simply that the winger was “unavailable” for a second successive game following a breach of club discipline. But, pressed if there was a way back for the winger, he added: “Of course there is.”

Asked about the resilience of his youthful team, Moyes added: “They’re so good, they give everything they’ve got. They’re a brilliant group of players. We beat Newcastle on Thursday night, and to beat them again today, it’s not an easy thing to do for any club.”

Jaissle acknowledged the reaction of Newcastle supporters to the performance and the result. “Big frustration, big disappointment,” he said. “Of course, the fans, they get frustrated like we are. We need to analyse it now in detail. It’s also clear that I have the responsibility, and I also take that as manager of this club. We need to do things better.”

Newcastle fans had made their feelings about the 3-1 Carabao Cup defeat away to Everton last Thursday clear to Jaissle, who has found himself under pressure early in his tenure. By the time he had gone on to the pitch at Hill Dickinson Stadium to acknowledge their backing, most of the 7,732 travelling supporters had headed for the exits, and St James’ Park emptied just as quickly after the home loss.

Eddie Howe was always going to be a hard act to follow given what he achieved in his first four years as head coach at St James’ Park, but the summer departures of big-name players, and his own 11th-hour arrival, has made the job even harder for Jaissle.

Frustration bubbled away beneath the surface at St James’ Park, a stadium which can be a cauldron when fans are given something to shout about. But the decibel levels were rarely raised in the first period. Newcastle’s Harvey Barnes cut inside late in the half, and an awkward deflection off Jarrad Branthwaite momentarily had Jordan Pickford worried, but, in truth, neither he nor Lukas Hornicek in the home goal were troubled in the first 45 minutes. Jake O’Brien and Harrison Armstrong had chances for Everton late in the half, but both shot wide.

Hornicek, however, was finally tested early in the second half – and a mistake from him handed Barry a goal. The goalkeeper let a shot from the left from Tyrique George squirm under his body, and Barry gratefully tapped the ball into an empty net.

Newcastle have given a number of soft goals away this season, and Jaissle conceded that his team had been caught “sleeping” by Everton, who pressed for a second goal before Yoane Wissa and Sean Steur were sent on by Jaissle.

Steur, after a hugely promising start to life at St James’ Park, has found himself on the bench in recent games to the bemusement of some supporters given how well he performed early in the season following his move from Ajax. Soon after Steur’s introduction, Barnes delivered a ball from the left which was met by Anthony Elanga at the back post. The ball rolled along the line, but did not fully cross it, and Everton cleared the danger.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

By now, St James’ Park had livened up, but the home team’s performance still lacked conviction in the final third.

Jaissle sent on Ramsey and Jacob Murphy for the last 15 minutes, but Newcastle found themselves pinned back by Everton, who were a threat on the break.

Half-chances came and went for Newcastle – who did not have a shot on target until the 86th minute, and also had Ramsey sent off for two stoppage-time yellow cards – as the travelling fans made themselves heard high up on Level 7.

The question some Newcastle fans are asking is just how high this team can finish above the Premier League’s relegation zone, as there are still big issues for Jaissle to address at both ends of the pitch ahead of what looks like being a challenging winter.

“The only way is togetherness, showing unity, and then the belief comes,” said Jaissle.

#807. Hellberg unsure of 'brilliant' Lankshear's England chances

Will Lankshear has only played the whole match in four of Middlesbrough's 13 Championship games

Middlesbrough head coach Kim Hellberg says he has too many other things to worry about than whether or not Will Lankshear receives a surprise England call-up.

Lankshear scored two more in the 3-0 win over Charlton Athletic to take his tally for Boro to 15 in 16 games, in all competitions, as they cemented their place at the top of the Championship.

The 21-year-old has claimed 13 strikes in as many Championship appearances following his summer move from Tottenham and Boro's form and his goalscoring exploits are receiving wider acclaim.

Last month England head coach Thomas Tuchel said he would never rule out picking players not in the top flight with their clubs, furthering the possibility that Lankshear could make the squad on Friday for the Nations League fixtures with Spain and Croatia later this month.

"I have no clue," said Hellberg, when asked if he thought Lankshear would find himself in Tuchel's reckoning.

"I have so many things to think about in terms of my own squad in terms of ins and outs and I have a brilliant squad working so hard so I let other people worry about that one."

The 'Kane-esque' striker Spurs may regret letting go

Lankshear has scored in all but one of his appearances at the Riverside and has scored two goals in four different matches.

Since the international break in September ended, he has been on fire, scoring seven times in five matches, including four in his last two in the victories over Bolton Wanderers and then Charlton Athletic.

The leading English scorer in the Premier League is Morgan Rogers with five, predominantly an attacking midfielder for Chelsea, while the English striker with most goals is Leeds United's Dominic Calvert-Lewin with four.

Lankshear even has more goals this season than England captain and Ballon d'Or winner Harry Kane, who has netted 12 in 14 games for Bayern Munich and the national team.

The Boro forward was part of the England Under-21 side last month, and Hellberg reckons he is already a better player than the one who moved to Teesside in the summer.

"Will is fantastic," the Swede told BBC Radio Tees. "He does everything every day. You can see the improvements through the season.

"When he arrived, he was unbelievable in the 18-yard box, and then he added on qualities in his defensive game that we worked with and pushed him to do, which he has done brilliantly and I am so happy with him getting a goal [against Charlton] from pressing high. He's a brilliant lad."

#805. Bottom club Sunderland to stick with manager Le Bris

Regis le Bris was appointed Sunderland manager in June 2024 when the club were in the Championship

Sunderland manager Regis le Bris is set to be given more time to turn things around despite his side's poor start to the Premier League season.

Le Bris is under pressure after Saturday's defeat at Coventry left the Black Cats bottom of the table with just one win from their first nine league matches.

However, club sources have told BBC Sport they believe the Frenchman can bring about an improvement in results.

Sunderland face Dinamo Zagreb in the Europa League at the Stadium of Light on Thursday, then host Chelsea in the league on Sunday before the international break begins.

Sunderland's paradox - San Siro trip amid relegation battle

Le Bris joined Sunderland from Lorient in 2024 and, in his first season in charge, oversaw promotion back to the Premier League after an eight-year absence.

The 50-year-old then guided the Black Cats to an impressive seventh-placed finish a year later, securing a spot in the Europa League.

It was the first time Sunderland had qualified for European competition in 53 years.

They have won two and drawn one of their Europa League league phase matches so far.

Le Bris' Sunderland were undoubtedly last season's surprise package, but they were also among the Premier League's biggest overperformers.

The Black Cats scored three more goals and conceded six fewer than their expected goals (xG) figures would have predicted.

They ranked towards the bottom of the league for possession and both the volume and quality of their shots, but stood out in defence.

Only Burnley and West Ham faced more attempts at goal, but the Wearsiders often restricted opponents to low-quality opportunities.

The average xG of the shots they faced was the second lowest in the league, while their save percentage of almost 72% was the second highest. That helps explain how Sunderland conceded the fourth fewest goals despite facing the third most shots.

It has been a very different story this season. Le Bris' side have gone from allowing the second-lowest xG per shot to the second highest.

The number of shots they face per game is almost unchanged, but opponents are creating far better chances. That has left goalkeeper Robin Roefs exposed, with Sunderland's 50% save rate the lowest in the top flight.

That defensive decline has been compounded by profligacy at the other end. The Black Cats rank 10th for xG but have scored six goals fewer than expected, making them among the Premier League's most wasteful finishers.

It was only five months ago that Sunderland became the first team promoted as play-off winners to qualify for Europe since Ipswich Town in 2001. But the Tractor Boys were relegated the following season and the Black Cats risk following suit unless Le Bris can address their problems at both ends.

The spoilerific final look at Denis Villeneuve's third and final sci-fi epic is loaded with action and drama that set it apart from Dune: Messiah's pages.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Dune: Part Three's marketing campaign has been a long and generous one, but Warner Bros. and Legendary Pictures knew an extra push was needed in order to compete with Avengers: Doomsday, as both sci-fi blockbusters will be releasing next to each other at Christmas. In its final trailer, Denis Villeneuve's threequel goes all out.

This isn't the first time a Dune: Part Three trailer has left us with more questions than answers, but the in-depth look at the character dynamics and plot beats that await will make longtime fans of Frank Herbert's works raise their eyebrows.

Messiah, the second installment in the book series, is a novel of long monologues and very tense conversations. Action has a place in it, but it's a more restrained and quieter book for the most part — one that deals with the consequences of Paul's (now a space dictator) originally well-meaning actions.

Of course, the cinematic medium requires a very different language, especially when the main reason why these movies have become blockbuster hits is that Villeneuve has expertly balanced the drama and large-scale action. So, it comes as no surprise that his take on Messiah is looking to bring Herbert's concluding thoughts on Paul Atreides (Timothée Chalamet) to life without sacrificing the grandeur that defined the first two movies.

More shocking to readers, of course, is Zendaya's (Chani) much larger role in this finale versus the book, where she was slightly sidelined with a more passive part. Paul's lover walking away from him at the end of Part Two was a major departure, and one that set her up for bigger things in the third entry. Considering how good Zendaya has been in the role so far, we consider this a win... unless Villeneuve completely bungles her arc in the final stretch.

Dune: Part Three emerges from the sand of Arrakis on December 18, 2026, only in cinemas.

#803. Kraft Drops Cinnamon Roll Mac & Cheese—and the Reactions Aren't Grate

Kraft dropped a surprising new lineup of limited-edition flavors—including mac and cheese that tastes like a cinnamon roll—which has garnered a big reaction from foodie fans.

The instant mac and cheese company was certainly thinking outside the box when they came up with one of their new limited-edition meals: Cinnamon Roll Kraft Mac & Cheese.

"Yep, you read that right," the brand teased on Instagram Nov. 2 alongside images of their festive new flavors' packaging. "Chili Crisp and Cinnamon Roll Kraft Mac & Cheese are available now for a limited time."

And while fans were cheesing over the announcement of another spicy flavor to follow their cult-classic jalapeño release in 2024, there were quite a few questions about the other product’s unexpectedly sweet noodle profile.

As one user put it, "Okay but why are you like this?" while another referred to the end of daylight saving's time when joking, "It was a time change, not April fools day!"

In fact, the experimental seasoning had the internet likening Kraft to mad scientists. To express their bewilderment, one X account replied to the news with a Jurassic Park meme in which Jeff Goldblum muses, "Your scientists were so preoccupied with whether they could, they didn't stop to think if they should.”

“Yall are out of your minds,” one person commented, as another quipped, "I’m calling the police.”

Still, some die-hard mac and cheese lovers were excited to roll with the dair-ing new addition.

"Everyone thought the apple pie one a year or two ago was weird, but it honestly was pretty good," one snack enthusiast replied on Instagram. "I’ll give cinnamon roll a shot!”

Another user admitted, "I... I need to try this. For science."

And as adventurous eaters know, noodle dishes that cater to the sweet tooth have been around for some time.

"Kraft cinnamon roll mac and cheese is going to be good and I'm not apologizing for that," an X post riffed. "Sweet plus cheese is not some new crime. Cheesecake exists, noodle kugel exists, half of you put syrup on a sausage biscuit."

#802. Villa drop legal action threat against Carragher

Jamie Carragher had upset Aston Villa and their fans with his comments

Aston Villa have dropped their threat of legal action against Sky Sports pundit Jamie Carragher.

On Friday, Villa had said they would initiate legal action against the former England defender for what they described as "unacceptable insults" made by Carragher on the Stick to Football podcast.

The former Liverpool defender linked Villa boss Unai Emery with replacing Michael Carrick at Manchester United and told fans to 'shut up' in response to their criticism of him.

Carragher apologised on Saturday for using "clumsy and wrong" language, and said his comments were "tongue in cheek".

Though Villa never initiated legal action against Carragher, they have now ended their threat to do so following his apology.

Emery, who joined Villa in 2022, has transformed the club's fortunes. The Spaniard has helped the club from battling relegation to Champions League regulars, while he also guided them to Europa League victory in 2026.

Carragher, though, suggested that Emery would want to manage a 'giant' club again, having previously managed Paris St-Germain and Arsenal.

"There is a chain in football, whether you like it or not," said Carragher.

"So Real Madrid will take Manchester United's best player, they did it with [Cristiano] Ronaldo. And there will be teams below Aston Villa, and they'll take their players or manager.

"Aston Villa will never be Manchester United."

Posting on social media on Saturday, Carragher retracted his comments.

"I'd like to apologise to Aston Villa, the owners and their fans," the pundit wrote.

"My language this week was clumsy and wrong.

"I can assure Villa fans it was tongue in cheek but I can understand it's not come across that way, so apologies."

It always seemed a more symbolic threat than one which would ever be followed through.

Carragher, while letting himself down with language, merely expressed an opinion and not a particularly extraordinary one.

While it shows naivety towards Emery's situation and the control he has at Villa it was hardly something to make headlines over.

It was one Villa should have let wash over them but not for the first time this season - or indeed in previous years - the club has chosen a combative position towards the media. Although, if owner Nassef Sawiris wants to do something there is very little some can do to change his mind.

Villa and Sawiris were defending their honour, as is their right, and they saw it as a slight on their ambition and how they could be perceived as lesser than United.

The idea of the traditional big six is one which irritates Villa, especially having won the Europa League and reached the Champions League for two of the past three seasons.

They have competed against those traditional sides - Arsenal, Liverpool, Chelsea, Manchester United, Manchester City and Tottenham - and have outperformed some of them at times. The threat towards Carragher was a sign of their determination to be seen as equals, even if it was misguided.

#801. Germany news: AfD's Weidel calls for major EU reforms

Far-right Alternative for Germany co-leader Alice Weidel reveals the party's plan to reform the EU. Meanwhile, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was in Berlin to talk to developers and investors. DW has more.

One of Weidel's reforms is for European parliamentarians to no longer be directly elected

Nvidia's Jensen Huang had words of encouragement for Europe's growing AI economy during a conference in Berlin

Germany's Finance Ministry has erroneously introduced an approved tax hike on tobacco products months before it was scheduled to come into effect

Germany's Bundesbank has forecast growth for the fourth quarter after a dip in the third quarter

This blog is now closed. Below is a round-up of top stories from and about Germany on Wednesday, October 21, 2026.

We'll be back with the latest headlines out of the country on Thursday. Tschüss!

Alice Weidel, the co-leader of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, has presented her party's proposals for a European Union that she said was "in severe need of reform" during a visit to the European Parliament in Strasbourg, saying they rested on three core pillars.

"We would like to rebuild and reform the European Union," she said. "We would like to found the European Union on three major principles: the first one is subsidiarity, the second one is responsibility, and the third one is sovereignty."

On subsidiarity — the idea that power should reside as close to the grassroots level as possible as much as possible — she said it was important to put the "competences" on the "lowest level of decision-making," saying "we don't want the state, or the [European] Commission — that is not elected — to intrude and disturb your private life in decision-making."

"I'm an economist, and for me, the European Union is not a group of sovereign states any more," Weidel said. She said that in sovereign states' parliaments, leaders were elected, "and so the decision-making on the sovereign level should be made in the national parliaments and not here, to be very clear."

This is already the case in the vast majority of core EU public policy areas. National governments decide foreign and defense issues, finance and health policy, education policy and much more. The notable exceptions Weidel objects to are fiscal policy and the primacy of EU law, but only after sovereign member states agree to them.

She said the European Commission was not elected but had a "legislative right of initiative," saying this was a "huge disturbance of checks and balances" and of a "democratic decision-making process."

Weidel accused the EU of failing to follow its own rules, for instance on sovereign debt and whether the European Central Bank should or can guarantee it, citing issues like this as questions of responsibility.

Finally, she reiterated her desire for "sovereign states to protect their borders," saying that "if the European Union is not capable of protecting our borders, the outer borders ... then it is a decision of the sovereign states to protect our national borders."

"If Schengen is over, if Schengen doesn't work, then we need to get out of Schengen and protect our borders," she said of the open-border zone within much of the EU.

She said that if the EU fails to protect the bloc's external borders, "we should have a veto right to opt out of this chaos."

While the EU maintains a border management agency, Frontex, national authorities are responsible for the external borders of the Schengen zone and the EU.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz criticized China for "unfair practices" in trade, and said he wants EU member states to balance out their trade deficits.

That elicited a bold comparison from a journalist who said, "You sound very much like Donald Trump."

A massive stage, all in black. A colorful laser light show. Upbeat music. AI-generated videos on a gigantic screen. On stage, just one man in a black leather jacket: Jensen Huang, the 63-year-old CEO of Nvidia, which manufactures superfast computer chips needed for AI data centers and happens to be the world's most valuable company.

The relaxed Nvidia boss set out his vision of the upcoming AI revolution and, of course, the products Nvidia has developed for the "second wave" of AI. The 4,000 attendees at Berlin's Tempodrom arena were thrilled by what Jensen Huang had to say (see entry below).

Huang said Germany and Europe could be part of the next industrial revolution — not as developers of AI language models or computer chips, but as producers of robots, machines, tools, and entire factories controlled by AI applications.

"You have to transfer AI into the real world of production," he said. Europe could use its data to train AI and develop customized models for automakers, pharmaceutical companies, and many small and medium-sized businesses.

Unsurprisingly, Nvidia offers all the AI software and hardware needed to get in on the action. A new addition to the Nvidia universe is a "Giga-Factory," which is housed in modular shipping containers and can be set up in just a few days or weeks anywhere with a suitable power grid.

There was also something for consumers: a high-performance laptop with a built-in AI agent that acts as a "friend and helper," capable of taking over tasks and programming new agents. Huang went on to demonstrate four small robot ducks that had been trained by this AI agent to perform cute tricks, which were met with laughter and applause.

But it wasn't all cheers. A woman in the audience interrupted a product demo to point out that AI is also used to control Russian drones. She was escorted out by security guards, but Huang assured the audience that he would speak with her later. He was keen to add that Nvidia has also developed a security system designed to keep AI agents in check and prevent misuse.

Nvidia is now valued at €5 trillion ($5.6 trillion) on the stock market. That is roughly equivalent to the total economic output of all of Germany in 2025.

The German military, known as the Bundeswehr, has rated the threat of sabotage against it as "significant," according to a reports by the Süddeutsche Zeitung (SZ) and public broadcaster WDR.

A spokesperson for the Defense Ministry pointed to several recent cases, including the discovery of a drone close to an airbase in Wunstorf and acts of sabotage against Navy ships.

The military is looking to increase security to counter the threat, with the ministry spokesperson naming increased surveillance at airports and military docks by soldiers or infrared cameras.

"The incidents highlight the ability that Russia has almost certainly had for a while now, as well as very likely the increased intention, to act against Bundeswehr forces and facilities, as well as partners such as Ukraine in Germany," SZ reported based on internal military analysis.

The aim is therefore "very likely an intention to degrade the current political and society-wide German support for Ukraine."

The ministry spokesperson also pointed out that the incidents did not mark a major change, with the military facing similar challenges over the past decades.

He said "automatic defense concepts" are in place for acute terror threats, but "we are not at that point."

German trade with Russia collapsed following the 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, especially due to the decision to cut all imports of Russian gas. However, some trade has continued.

According to the German Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), German imports of Russian goods were down by 96.4% in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period in 2021.

This amounted to €500 million ($561 million) in 2026, down from €15 billion. German exports to Russia were also down, but still significant, reaching €3.4 billion in the first six months of 2026. However, this was about a quarter of the exports in the same period in 2021.

Pharmaceutical products made up more than 40% of German exports to Russia, with machinery, food and animal feed also being exported in smaller quantities.

Jensen Huang, the head of chip manufacturing giant Nvidia, was speaking at a company conference for developers and investors in Berlin's Tempodrom auditorium on Wednesday.

He was seeking to encourage Europe to build out its data center infrastructure and touted Nvidia's modular tools to help speed up that process.

"Europe's AI economy is starting, and it's accelerating, and it's great to see," Huang said.

He promoted a new design for a ready-made modular computing center that comes in a box akin to a shipping container and that could make it possible to construct a data center in a matter of days. Huang said it "will change the way people build AI centers."

Nvidia has invested $10 billion (€8.9 billion) in European startups over the past year, the Nvidia boss said.

Europe has fallen behind the US and China in terms of building up data centers and is currently home to around 5% of the world's AI computing capacity in comparison to 75% in the US. This capacity is required to train AI models and its lack is seen as a major obstacle for European developers.

Most current data centers are reliant on Nvidia GPUs to run.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A spokesperson for Germany's Federal Financial Ministry on Wednesday addressed confusion surrounding the implementation of a new tobacco tax saying, "The tax increase in the law's wording was approved to go into effect on January 1, 2027, that remains the case."

The spokesperson confirmed that the mix-up over when the new law would take effect resulted from a technical error that put the law on the books immediately rather than January 1 as intended.

The issue stemmed from a mistake in the government's original writing of the law.

Customs officials have reportedly been informed and the Financial Ministry's website makes clear that the price increase will not be charged until the beginning of the new year.

"Gen Z regelt" — or Gen Z's Got It — a youth initiative, has called for mass protests in 21 cities across Germany on Saturday, October 31; including Berlin, Cologne, Hamburg and Munich.

Thousands are expected to participate in demonstrations protesting "broken schools and austerity," as well as the cost of living, social injustice, military conscription and climate change.

French protests that exploded in violence and rampant destruction of private and public property this weekend also grew out of student frustration over the national school system and soon included numerous unions, groups and individuals voicing anger over a number of issues.

Gen Z regelt's website clearly states that the initiative is "against all violence," whether directed at people or property.

Police say they are "vigilant and relaxed," adding that they intend to protect people's right to congregate and express their opinions.

Still, images of massive damage and public violence from France, Italy and Spain have raised concerns among domestic policymakers and police, who have warned against allowing the protests to be hijacked by left-wing extremists.

Andreas Roßkopf, head of the German Federal Police's GdP union, made clear that officers would deal harshly with riots and rioters, telling the Rheinische Post newspaper on Wednesday, "State, but also federal police, will offer a firm and decisive response" to any trouble.

Roßkopf also warned that radicals and extremists could insert themselves among demonstrators in order to "attack police" or "simply be destructive."

The Bundesbank, Germany's central bank, has said it is expecting to see an uptick in growth for Europe's biggest economy in the fourth quarter.

"German economic output is likely to improve again markedly in the fourth quarter," the bank said in its monthly report on Wednesday. "However, the future economic recovery depends, not least, on the development of the war in the Middle East."

The optimistic outlook follows a dip in the third quarter, which the bank chalked up largely to this summer's drought that caused such low water levels in the Rhine River, an artery in western Germany for industry, that most ships could not travel.

"The low water levels are also likely to continue to have a negative impact on foreign trade via European ports as a result of restrictions on inland water transport," the bank wrote.

The forecast will be welcomed by the Merz government as it has struggled to boost the economy after two consecutive years of recession followed by weak growth in 2025.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said he does not think Europe is on course for a trade war with China while acknowledging what he called "unfair practice" on the part of Beijing.

Speaking at a business conference in Berlin, Merz said the imbalance did not mean "the beginning of a war, of a trade war with China. We are looking for peaceful solutions, but the level for that is fair trade."

The German chancellor has been pushing for the EU to be better prepared for trade disputes with China, including calling for a means to quickly exclude non-EU countries from the EU's single market if they flood it with cheap goods.

Merz said the EU needs to be able "to protect our markets and defend ourselves against those who don't play by the rules."

"Anyone who disrupts the functioning of the markets through unfair subsidies, overcapacities, aggressive pricing, or artificially undervalued currencies must expect a response," he said.

That includes tools that "enable us to respond swiftly and vigorously to targeted attacks on our industry and supply chain, with the idea being that in the best case we will not have to use it."

Germany has a rather generous parental allowance system in comparison to many countries, with parents being able to take off 14 months, if each parent takes at least two months off, with the government paying up to €1,800 (just over $2,000) a month during that period.

However, this system has become the subject of a planned reform under the government of Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

The plan is to reduce the maximum amount of full-time paid parental leave to 12 months. With three months each reserved for both parents and the remaining six months free to be divided up however the parents choose. It also raises the minimum payment from €300 to €330 and the maximum from €1,800 to €1,900.

The government's aim is to make cuts to help the Ministry for Family Affairs reach its savings target of €1.6 billion, while also encouraging more fathers to take parental leave. Currently, fewer than half of fathers in Germany take parental leave.

Now the Ifo Institute for Economic Research has cast doubts on the government's savings plan.

"The savings target and the goal of increasing fathers’ participation in the planned parental allowance reform are at odds with each other. The higher the number of fathers who are motivated to participate by the reform, the less the government saves," Ifo researcher Kyra Puteanus said.

The institute estimates savings of around €880 million from November 2027, when the reform comes into effect. However, if more fathers, who generally earn more and thus are able to request the highest payment, do take up the parental leave, this will quickly reduce the savings, with Ifo predicting that even if the uptake by fathers only increases by 1%, savings will fall to €597 million. An increase of 3.1% would undo any savings from the reform, according to the institute.

"Since 2010, however, the share of fathers receiving parental allowance has almost doubled. A rapid increase can therefore not be ruled out, especially if months are otherwise forfeited," Ifo researcher Franziska Nuernbergk said.

The Israel Defense Forces (IFD) said in a post on X that they have killed Tamer Mohammad Ibrahim Al-Zabaq, a member of the Hamas terror group who was involved in the October 7 attacks.

The post said that al-Zabaq had been one of the men responsible for the abduction of Shani Louk, a dual German-Israeli national.

Louk was initially thought to have been taken hostage following the Hamas-led attacks but it was later confirmed that she had been killed.

In the immediate aftermath of the terror attacks, pictures and videos shared online showed a young woman, believed to be Shani, lying face down in a pick-up truck driven by militants. It was unclear from the footage whether she was alive.

The IDF also accused Al-Zabaq of operating to "restore Hamas' military capabilities, in systematic violation of the ceasefire."

"The terrorist was eliminated in order to remove the threat he posed," the IDF said.

The claims in the X post could not be independently verified.

Israel has carried out numerous deadly strikes on Gaza since the ceasefire came into effect just over a year ago.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, addressing the Business Global Dialogue summit in Berlin on Wednesday, renewed calls for US President Donald Trump to invite South Africa (a G20 member) to the upcoming G20 summit that he will host in Miami this December.

"Whoever talks about the future of the global economy must include all important partners. Of course Africa belongs at the table," he said, adding: "The African Union is a G20 member, as is South Africa. That is why I urgently insist that South Africa be represented at the G20 summit."

Merz made a similar plea last year, when Trump angrily insisted that he would not invite South Africa to the annual summit of the 20 leading industrial and emerging economies.

Trump has accused South Africa of committing genocide on white farmers and dismissed South African pushback against his repeated claim. The anti-immigrant president also took the unusual step of offering South Africans political asylum in the US — as long as they are white.

The US President is apparently less bothered by wars of aggression, extending an invitation to President Vladimir Putin to come to Miami, despite Russia being thrown out of the G8 — now G7 — over its 2014 invasion and annexation of Ukraine's Crimea.

Beyond his plea for South Africa's inclusion, Merz said he would travel to the US with what he called a "Miami Growth Agenda" aimed at slashing bureaucracy, pushing structural reforms and making investment easier.

"Those" he said, "are the prerequisites for new economic growth and prosperity, not only in Germany, but globally."

Russian FSB agents have arrested a German national, accusing him of being a mercenary under contract with the Ukrainian army.

"The Federal Security Service of the Russian Federation has detained a German citizen who is a serving member of the Armed Forces of Ukraine," said a statement cited by Russian news agencies.

The FSB says the man, whom they described as a sniper, previously fought in Afghanistan and Syria as well as in Ukraine between 2016 and 2018.

They say he arrived in Ukraine last November and signed a three-year contract with the Ukrainian army before deserting over unpaid wages.

Last week, the FSB arrested a Swedish national whom Russian authorities also accused of fighting on Kyiv's behalf.

Russia has arrested hundreds of foreign nationals that it accuses of "espionage," "sabotage" or "treason" to long prison sentences since it began its invasion of neighboring Ukraine.

A number of foreign nationals have also been jailed over supposed "mercenary activity."

The Shenlong space plane can be seen docked to another satellite that has its solar panels deployed.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A U.S. military intelligence agency has released an incredible new photograph of China's secretive space plane, showing it docked to another spacecraft in orbit.

The photograph was taken in 2024 by Vantor's WorldView 3 satellite, from a distance of 56 miles (90 kilometers). Ground-based observers have previously photographed Shenlong in orbit, but this new photo from Vantor, taken from space, reveals new details about the mysterious spacecraft in stunning clarity, with a resolution of 4.5 centimeters (1.8 inches) per pixel. The image was included in a new report released by the Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) assessing the scope and breadth of adversary threats in space.

In the image, the robotic Shenlong space plane can be seen docked to another satellite that has its solar panels deployed. It's not yet known which satellite that may have been. Shenlong's payload bay doors can also be seen in the photograph, in an open position.

Those payload doors may offer clues about what Shenlong is doing on its fourth mission, which launched in February 2026. China's space agency has stated only that Shenlong helps test technologies that "will pave the way for more convenient and affordable round-trip methods for the peaceful use of space in the future."

But observers have seen Shenlong release other objects while in orbit, such as in June 2026, when American space intelligence company LeoLabs reported that itdetected a new object in the vicinity of the space plane.

"Following additional observations across our global network and analysis via LeoLabs Delta, we have independently cataloged this object and assessed with high confidence that it was released from the Chinese space plane," LeoLabs stated at the time. "This activity is consistent with sub-satellite deployments conducted by the space plane in previous missions."

A similar event happened during Shenlong's third mission, which ended in 2024. On its second mission in 2023, the space plane also released an object and may have conducted what are known as proximity and rendezvous operations, in which two spacecraft maneuver close to one another.

It may have been that the spacecraft was releasing unnecessary hardware before landing, however. Like all things military space, few details have been released to the public about Shenlong's operations.

The United States, similarly, operates a secretive robotic space plane, the Boeing-built X-37B, and rarely releases concrete details about its capabilities or its missions. In February 2025, the U.S. Space Force released its first photo of the X-37B in space, offering a rare glimpse at the space plane in operation. The photo appeared to show it in a high Earth orbit with what appear to be its payload bay doors open.

In 2023, Space Force released its first official painting, depicting an X-37B-like space plane in orbit above Earth, intercepting another satellite.

With China and the United States currently jockeying for the lead in what many observers have called a new Space Race, rare glimpses like these images may be a way of militaries and intelligence agencies of teasing capabilities without fully revealing them to the public.

Brett is curious about emerging aerospace technologies, alternative launch concepts, military space developments and uncrewed aircraft systems. Brett's work has appeared on Scientific American, The War Zone, Popular Science, the History Channel, Science Discovery and more. Brett has degrees from Clemson University and the University of North Carolina at Charlotte. In his free time, Brett enjoys skywatching throughout the dark skies of the Appalachian mountains.
