#730. Russia's attacks on Ukraine's capital, Kyiv, are intensifying. DW asked people on the ground what life is like

Russia's attacks on the Ukrainian capital are hitting harder and more frequently, making 2026 one of the long war's bloodiest years for Kyiv. DW asked people on the ground what life is like.

Until a few months ago, life was relatively peaceful in Kyiv when compared with the situation near the war's front lines elsewhere in Ukraine. Now, as Russia expands its attacks on the capital, Kyiv has increasingly become a front-line city.

With too few shelters for the 4 million residents of Kyiv, subway stations double as makeshift dormitories. Starting at about 10 every night, people create sleeping areas with mattresses and small tents. Children snuggle up to adults; pets seek comfort from their owners or find a spot among strangers between the cold walls.

"We're alive," Halyna told DW, holding her 5-year-old son, Roman, close. "We've been lucky once again." Most evenings — even when no air-raid siren has sounded — she takes the boy to the nearest subway station. Her apartment is located in the Lukyanivka district, which Russia has systematically targeted over the war's four years and eight months.

In September, 14-year-old Daniel Umanskyj was doing homework in his room when a Russian drone struck the apartment building in the central district of Pechersk. A neighbor named Vlad happened to be in the hallway with his daughter at the time of the strike. "We were late that day — and this saved our lives," Vlad said. "Daniel's death is a tragedy." He added: "These sick monsters don't care who they kill." Flowers have been planted in front of the damaged apartment building in memory of Daniel.

Russia also targets places where children gather. In early October, a drone struck a school building  in southwestern Kyiv. Fortunately, pupils and teachers were already in shelters at the time.

"We've been teaching all the pupils in person because we have a large shelter that can accommodate more than 500 students," Valentyna Chorna, the school's principal, told DW. As there is enough space in the shelter for everyone, students in the first through ninth grades are able to go to school, she said.

Whether classes take place depends not only on the decision of the parents and the school administration: It also depends on whether shelters are available and how long the air-raid siren continues to sound. If an alarm sounds in the morning while children are still at home, they may not be able to go to school that day.

"This is an enormous burden for parents," said a colleague from the DW bureau in Kyiv, whose daughter attends school. "You have to go to work — and the child stays home alone."

"Even the walk to school is dangerous because an air-raid alarm can go off at any time," she said. Her daughter attends a school not far from the Antonov aircraft factory. "One day she texted me: ‘You can't imagine what a huge explosion that was!'" she said. "I don't know if something was shot down or if there was a strike somewhere." She added: "Things like that really scare children." And staying home brings its own risks.

In September, a Russian drone struck their building. The apartment itself wasn't damaged, and her daughter was at school that morning, but it was another reminder of just how much survival has become a matter of luck. When an air-raid siren sounds, no one knows who will be spared, she said.

Russia's attacks have become deadlier in 2026. According to the military administration in Kyiv, 140 people were killed in the capital during the first eight months of the year, compared with 172 for all of 2025. If this trend continues, 2026 could become Kyiv's deadliest year since the start of the Russian invasion in 2022.

Attacks on warehouses have led to shortages in supermarkets on a scale not seen since the early months of the war. At the end of September, emergency power outages resumed in Kyiv. The subway was paralyzed by a Russian attack. Given the strikes on the energy infrastructure, it is unclear how the capital can reliably supply residents with heat, electricity and water during the upcoming winter.

Despite Russia's attempts to render Kyiv uninhabitable, 72% of the city's residents said in September that they are prepared to endure the war for as long as necessary, the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology reported in early October. The authorities are striving to maintain normal life in the city, where the curfew has been shortened and now runs from 1 a.m. to 5 a.m.

Some facilities have even been allowed to continue operating during "yellow" alerts. During "red" alerts, however, people must immediately seek shelter: This  could mean ballistic missiles, cruise missiles or massive combined attacks.

#729. Justin Timberlake to Release 4-Part Docuseries That Includes Janet Jackson as a Guest

The project is set to arrive on Apple TV by the end of the year.

Justin Timberlake has some things to get off his chest. Variety reported Monday (Nov. 2) that the pop star has a four-part “tell-all” docuseries in the works at Apple TV, featuring none other than Janet Jackson as a guest.

The project is reportedly expected to arrive on the streamer in December, with no further details available at press time aside from one of the discussion topics that will be included. With Miss Jackson onboard, the doc will almost certainly look back on the pair’s infamous 2004 Super Bowl controversy, which involved Timberlake exposing her breast on live TV — aka the incident from which the term “wardrobe malfunction” was born.

Billboard has reached out to Timberlake’s reps for comment.

The project comes amid a reflective chapter for the former *NSYNC boy bander, who made headlines in 2021 with a public apology to Jackson acknowledging the disparity in how they were respectively treated after the Super Bowl controversy. “I am deeply sorry for the times in my life where my actions contributed to the problem, where I spoke out of turn, or did not speak up for what was right,” Timberlake wrote. “I understand that I fell short in these moments and in many others and benefited from a system that condones misogyny and racism.”

Also in his apology, Timberlake expressed remorse for the disrespectful ways in which he’d previously spoken about Britney Spears following their breakup in 2002.

Things got rocky for JT a few years later in 2024, when he was arrested on suspicion of driving while intoxicated in the Hamptons. He ultimately pleaded guilty to a lesser impaired-driving charge, and the singer was sentenced to 25 hours of community service.

“It’s been a tough week,” Timberlake told fans at one of his Forget Tomorrow World Tour concerts shortly afterward. “I know I’m hard to love sometimes, but you keep loving me right back.”

After the trek ended the following year, the star revealed another challenge he’d been facing behind the scenes: Lyme disease.

“Living with this can be relentlessly debilitating, both mentally and physically,” he wrote in a statement at the time. “When I first got the diagnosis I was shocked for sure. But, at least I could understand why I would be onstage and in a massive amount of nerve pain or, just feeling crazy fatigue or sickness.”

Timberlake hasn’t dropped an album since 2024, reaching No. 4 on the Billboard 200 with Everything I Thought It Was. He did, however, recently team up with Quavo on the new song “House Music,” which dropped in early October.

#728. Mckenna Grace Says She’s Terrified to Do Nudity for Roles

"I definitely don’t do nudity or very hypersexual things," the 'The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping' star says.

Mckenna Grace is getting candid about the types of roles she’s not interested in at this point in her career.

The 20-year-old actress, who next stars as Maysilee Donner in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, recently told Cosmopolitan, “I definitely don’t do nudity or very hypersexual things.”

“I respect anybody who can, but it’s terrifying to me,” she explained. “I don’t know if that’ll ever change. It’s not like I only do wholesome things — my character literally gets gutted by Ghostface in [Scream 7] — but my dream is to try and be a Disney princess someday.” Related Stories Movies 'End of Oak Street' Box Office Aims to Take Bite Out of 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' Movies 'PAW Patrol: The Dino Movie' Review: Busy New Entry in Pup Franchise Is Exactly What You'd Expect

Grace, who already has dozens of film and television projects to her name, rose to fame as a child actor. After landing her first commercial at age five, she quickly began making a name for herself before she was even a teenager with her roles in The Young and the Restless, Gifted, I, Tonya and The Haunting of Hill House, among others.

The Regretting You actress also opened up about how she navigated the transition from kid to adult on set, admitting she enjoys having “a bit more ownership” over her roles now.

“As a kid on set, you’re expected to act like an adult until you’re on camera. Then you’re a kid until everybody is mad at you because you’re acting like a kid,” she said. “Now it’s cool to be an adult and be able to give my opinion and have a bit more ownership over characters. I’ve really enjoyed sitting down with producers and pitching all my ideas.”

As Grace gets settled into adulthood, she’s already landed several major projects, from Regretting You to Five Nights at Freddy’s 2 to Scream 7, and she’s now preparing for the global release of Sunrise on the Reaping on Nov. 20.

When The Hollywood Reporter caught up with the actress at the film’s U.K. premiere in October, she admitted that taking on the role of Maysilee was “daunting and insane,” especially after seeing all the early fancasts for her to play Haymitch’s (Joseph Zada) arena ally.

“I think that what eased some of the pressure was the fact that people seemed to respond mostly nicely to my casting, which is not always the case,” Grace said. “That meant so much to me that the fanbase liked me as Maysilee because I was like, ‘I don’t even know if I like myself as Maysilee! How am I gonna do this justice?’ Like, taking on something like this in a franchise that I care so deeply about and a character that means everything to me. It’s been so daunting and insane.”

The LLRV was a bizarre, four-legged flying contraption commonly known as the "Flying Bedstead" used by Apollo astronauts for moon landing practice.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On October 30, 1964, NASA's Lunar Landing Research Vehicle, or LLRV, took to the skies for the first time.

The LLRV was a bizarre, four-legged flying contraption commonly known as the "Flying Bedstead." NASA used it to simulate moon landings and liftoffs on Earth to prepare for Apollo 11, the first crewed lunar landing.

The first person to give it a whirl was the X-15 pilot Joe Walker. During this test flight, he reached an altitude of about 10 feet, and he hovered there for about a minute. He did this two more times that same day. In all, he completed more than 30 test flights with the LLRV.

These test flights took place at NASA's Dryden Flight Research Center in Edwards, California. That facility has since been renamed the Armstrong Flight Research Center after Neil Armstrong, who also piloted — and famously crashed — the "Flying Bedstead" before he went to the moon.

Over 60 years ago this LLRV test flight was a critical step toward landing humans on the moon for the first time, a historic moment that both served an important political purpose while also showcasing the result of monumental scientific and technical progress.

While images from this test flight might look like the team are having a bit of fun out in the desert, and perhaps they were, it was also deadly serious. The astronauts who signed onto these crewed missions were doing something that had never been attempted. They were putting their lives on the line for this progress, and this testing was a major piece in reassuring them and NASA that lunar landing could be accomplished, and safely.

Today, as we return humans to the moon with NASA's Artemis program, we see parallels between testing done over 60 years ago and testing today. Right now, SpaceX and Blue Origin are testing their lunar landers for crewed lunar landings in the near-future. While we have now been to the moon and have safely and successfully landed humans before, these tests remain critical for the safety and success of the missions.

As an editor with over 10 years of experience in science journalism she has previously written for Scholastic Classroom Magazines, MedPage Today and The Joint Institute for Computational Sciences at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. After studying physics at the University of Tennessee in her hometown of Knoxville, she earned her graduate degree in Science, Health and Environmental Reporting (SHERP) from New York University. Hanneke joined the Space.com team in 2016 as a staff writer and producer, covering topics including spaceflight and astronomy. She currently lives in Seattle, home of the Space Needle, with her cat and two snakes. In her spare time, Hanneke enjoys exploring the Rocky Mountains, basking in nature and looking for dark skies to gaze at the cosmos.

#726. ‘Robopocalypse’ TV Show in the Works With Ron Howard, Akiva Goldsman

The 2011 novel was once going to be a movie from Steven Spielberg, who will serve as an executive producer on the project via his Amblin Entertainment.

Imagine Entertainment and Weed Road are developing a series based on the 2011 book by Daniel H. Wilson, with Imagine’s Ron Howard attached to direct the pilot and Weed Road’s Akiva Goldsman set to showrun and write the pilot. No network or streamer is yet involved.

The book shot to fame in the early 2010s when Steven Spielberg optioned it to direct even before it was published, with a draft of the script written by Drew Goddard. Spielberg flirted with the book for years, with Anne Hathaway and Chris Hemsworth attached to star. Spielberg eventually postponed the project indefinitely in 2014, with Michael Bay coming aboard in 2018 to direct. That version didn’t get made either. Related Stories Movies Ron Howard to be Honored at 2026 Critics Choice Documentary Awards Movies Netflix Acquires Ron Howard's 'Avedon' Documentary for 2026 Release, Awards Push (Exclusive)

Now, Spielberg’s Amblin Entertainment will exec produce the show. Imagine’s Brian Grazer and Jeb Brody and Weed Pictures’ Greg Lessans and Rachel Wizenberg will lead the development with Goldsman and Howard.

The novel is more relevant than ever amid current fears of AI causing the death of humanity. It centers on humanity’s war against robots controlled by a powerful AI, and per the logline: “Not far into our future, the dazzling technology that runs our world turns against us. At Zero Hour—the moment the robots attack—the human race is almost annihilated, but as its scattered remnants regroup, humanity for the first time unites in a determined effort to fight back. Brilliantly conceived and amazingly detailed, Robopocalypse is an action-packed epic with chilling implications about the real technology that surrounds us.”

“Robopocalypse has all the scale and suspense of a major action story, but what drew me to it are the thought-provoking themes and humanity at its center,” said Howard in a statement. “Daniel created a future that feels both startling and increasingly plausible, with characters who must figure out what connects us when the technology we rely on turns against us. I am also thrilled to work with Akiva again. We have shared some incredibly meaningful creative experiences, and this feels like the right story to bring us back together.”

Howard and Goldsman are longtime collaborators, dating back to the film A Beautiful Mind, which won Howard best director and best picture Oscars, and nabbed Goldsman the best adapted screenplay statue.

And they found a big hit with The Da Vinci Code, their adaptation of Dan Brown’ novel. The 2006 movie topped $760 million globally.

#725. TWS: The Beauty of Growing Up Unscripted

With their second single album TO US, SHINYU, DOHOON, YOUNGJAE, HANJIN, JIHOON & KYUNGMIN open up about growing up & embracing imperfections.

Since their debut in 2024, TWS have captured the spirit of youth through their signature sound: “Boyhood Pop.” From the excitement of first encounters to the joy of moving forward together, their music has always carried a celebratory energy.

But after more than two years in the spotlight, SHINYU, DOHOON, YOUNGJAE, HANJIN, JIHOON and KYUNGMIN are beginning to see the stories of growing up they’ve long told through their music in a different light.

Their second single album, TO US, which arrived Monday (Nov. 2), turns its attention to the less polished moments along the way. Rather than focusing solely on the highs of youth, TWS now speak more openly about mistakes, regrets, and self-doubt, adding a new layer of complexity through their own experiences. It’s not a rejection of the optimism that has defined their sound, but an expansion of what growing up means to them: recognizing that the moments that didn’t go according to plan have become just as much a part of their story.

In conversation with Billboard Korea, the six members reflect on how they’ve changed since debut, what they’ve learned about themselves and one another, and how they hope to expand their musical identity. When asked what they’d tell their past selves and the group they’ve become, they didn’t talk about setting bigger goals. Instead, they speak of keeping going, taking care of themselves, and growing at their own pace.

For a group that has always found reasons to celebrate through music, TO US offers another: the beauty of embracing who they are, imperfections and all.

What stands out about TO US is how it embraces the mistakes and regrets that come with growing up, rather than treating them as things to hide. Looking back since your debut, is there a moment that felt disappointing at the time, but that you now recognize as something that helped you grow?

JIHOON: When we first debuted, there were so many things I wasn’t as good at as I am now — whether it was my stamina, how I communicated with fans onstage, or my singing and dancing. With each comeback, I’d set small goals for myself, thinking, “I want to do better at this next time.”

But I failed a lot. It hurt when I couldn’t achieve the goals I’d set for myself. Looking back, though, I see those moments as some of the brightest and most precious. They became the motivation to keep working hard, and I think that connects closely with the message of this album.

YOUNGJAE: Like JIHOON, I remember being nervous about every single performance when we first debuted. I wasn’t nearly as comfortable onstage as I am now, and with everything still so unfamiliar, there are things I wish I’d done better.

But I think the freshness and innocence of those early days came through in our performances, too. Our fans appreciated that side of us, and now I look back on those moments as really good memories.

The final chorus of “Call My Name” carries a celebratory feeling that also runs through earlier TWS songs like “hey! hey!” and “Last Festival.” Even with the regrets and uncertainties of youth, there’s a sense of celebrating who you are in the moment. For TWS today, what kinds of moments feel worth celebrating?

DOHOON: The first thing that comes to mind is simply enjoying music without any worries. That’s what a celebration feels like to me.

SHINYU: For me, it’s being onstage, making eye contact with the members and connecting with them while we perform. Those moments really feel like a celebration..

KYUNGMIN: We recently went on tour, and performing the stages we’d prepared in different countries felt like a celebration in itself.

Does that feeling ever extend beyond the stage into your everyday lives?

SHINYU: Definitely! Like when I finish work and get to eat something delicious that I love. That’s one of my favorite ways to relieve stress, so even a moment like that can feel like a celebration.

Since your debut, TWS has built a distinct musical identity, with a bright, refreshing sound that listeners have come to associate with the group. Having such a recognizable identity is a strength, but have you ever felt that expectations of what “sounds like TWS” could also become a boundary when you want to try something new?

JIHOON: I’m happy that people associate us with a particular sound. It means we’ve successfully communicated the musical identity we wanted to establish when we debuted. But I also believe we have so many more cards we haven’t played yet.

Rather than feeling pressured by those expectations, I’m excited to show what else we can do. We’ve already explored different genres through our concert performances, and it’s been really rewarding to reveal those sides of ourselves. I see our existing identity as something to build on, not something that limits us.

Looking ahead, how would you like to expand TWS’ musical identity?

YOUNGJAE: I want us to keep telling different kinds of stories through Boyhood Pop, just as we have with TO US. What matters to me is finding messages that feel true to who we are as TWS and expressing them through our music, in our own way.

You mentioned wanting to tell more diverse stories through Boyhood Pop. With TO US, what message do you most want to share with 42s?

YOUNGJAE: I think our title track, “Call My Name” (“내 이름을 불러줘”), captures that message. We wanted to express the idea that our performance begins the moment 42s call our names.

Our fans are always calling out to us and coming to see us, and this song is our way of responding to them. I think there’s something really beautiful about that.

TO US reveals a more honest, less polished side of youth. More than two years since your debut, you’ve also come to know yourselves and one another better, including the parts that aren’t always perfect. To close with the album’s title, if you could say something to yourselves and to the “us” that has come this far together, what would it be?

JIHOON: There’s something I’ve been saying a lot lately: “Keep going.”

We’re always giving each other feedback and looking for ways to improve, even during practice. Of course, there are difficult moments when we wonder, “Can we really do this?” There are still so many mountains left for us to climb. But I want to tell us to keep going, just as we have been.

YOUNGJAE: Mine would be “Take care.” (Laughs.) We’re all still in our early twenties, so we have plenty of energy to keep working hard. But with our busy schedules and sometimes not getting enough sleep, it can take a toll on our bodies.

I believe we need to be healthy, both physically and mentally, to accomplish everything we want to do. So I’d tell myself and the members, “Take care.”

SHINYU: Mine is similar to JIHOON’s. I’d say, “Just keep doing what you’ve been doing.” We’re always finding things to improve and giving each other feedback, like JIHOON said. But I also want to remind us, “You’re already doing well. Just keep doing what you’ve been doing.”

HANJIN: “At our own pace, in our own TWS way.” Since debut, we’ve been meeting 42s and performing so often that everything can feel a little rushed at times. I want to remind us that we don’t have to hurry. We can keep moving forward at our own pace, in our own TWS way.

DOHOON: I’d say, “Let’s focus on the good things.” Once you start having negative thoughts, it’s easy to get caught up in them. Lately, as we’ve entered our third year, I’ve been trying to find more happiness in everyday life and appreciate the little things that bring me joy.

KYUNGMIN: I don’t think anyone is perfect. What matters is recognizing where you can improve and continuing to work on those things. And I think it’s just as important to find joy in the process.

You’ve been TWS’ leader since debut. More than two years into that role, how has your understanding of what makes a good leader changed from when you first started?

SHINYU: When we first debuted, I thought being a good leader meant standing at the front and leading the members. But over time, I’ve come to realize just how much each member means to me. Now, I believe a good leader is someone who brings everyone together and supports them from behind.

You once mentioned that loving yourself was difficult. With TO US exploring the idea of accepting even the imperfect parts of ourselves, does that feeling still resonate with you today? How has your relationship with yourself changed?

SHINYU: I still find it difficult to love myself. I tend to hold myself to very high standards. But seeing how much the members and 42s love me makes me want to learn to love myself, little by little.

What does it take for you to genuinely tell yourself, “I did well this time”? Has the standard you hold yourself to changed over the past two years?

DOHOON: I like to reflect on my day before going to sleep. If I feel I’ve made good use of my time, I can go to bed feeling happy. When we first debuted, I had a lot of worries and tended to blame myself for things. These days, I’m learning to be kinder to myself and accept the parts of me that aren’t perfect.

Since your debut, have there been times when you’ve been particularly conscious of how others see or evaluate you? How do you distinguish between other people’s perceptions of you and the way you see yourself today?

DOHOON: Of course, I care about how others see me. But even when people compliment me, I can’t feel completely satisfied unless I’ve met my own expectations. That’s just the kind of person I am. I’m always trying to meet my own standards and push beyond them.

You’ve talked about being drawn to emotionally resonant music. Beyond music itself, where do you find inspiration — in books, films or everyday life? Have you ever wanted to turn those feelings into something you’ve created yourself?

YOUNGJAE: I find a lot of inspiration in films, dramas, and books. They let me experience emotions and situations I might never encounter in my own life. Sometimes I seek out certain works because I want to explore those feelings or find inspiration, while other times I come across something that moves me unexpectedly.

Is there a particular work that’s stayed with you recently?

YOUNGJAE: Actually, our own music video. I was genuinely happy throughout the filming process. You’ll understand when you see it, but it was a chance for both us and the director to try something new.

Music video shoots can be demanding, and this one certainly wasn’t easy. Still, even during the difficult moments, I kept thinking about how much fun I was having and how precious the experience felt. I remember feeling incredibly happy just to be there.

Would you ever want to express those kinds of emotions through music you’ve created yourself?

YOUNGJAE: HANJIN and I performed a unit song at our concert, and I poured as much of who I am right now into it as I could. So in a way, if you’re wondering what those feelings would sound like in my own music, I think that song already has the answer.

You often come across as someone who brings a sense of stability to those around you. But when you’re the one feeling uncertain or emotionally unsettled, what helps you find your balance again?

YOUNGJAE: The members and people around me often tell me I’m emotionally stable, but I have plenty of moments when I feel shaken, too. Sometimes I feel really small.

What helps me through those moments is believing in the people who believe in me. Knowing there are people who care about me and trust me makes me want to do better for them. It gives me a reason to work harder, find my footing again and keep moving forward.

Since your debut, you’ve had to learn and grow in many ways while already performing and working as a member of TWS. Has that ever brought a sense of pressure or urgency to improve quickly? Looking back, how have those experiences shaped you?

HANJIN: Rather than saying I’ve grown a lot, I’d say there are many things I’ve gotten better at. Korean is probably the biggest one. When I first came to Korea, I couldn’t speak the language at all, which made both communicating with others and learning new things really difficult. But with help from the members and my teachers, I’ve gradually become more comfortable with it.

Is there a side of yourself that you feel people haven’t fully seen yet? What would you like to show more of in the future?

HANJIN: There are two things. First, I want to keep showing better performances onstage with the members.

The second is more personal. I think people usually see me as someone who’s cheerful, laughs a lot, and loves to talk. But lately, I’ve been wanting to show a calmer, more composed side of myself. I’ve always been the type to rush into things, and even when I try to slow down, it doesn’t always come naturally. With this comeback, I hope I can start showing that side of myself, little by little.

You’ve devoted much of your life to dance and have spoken about wanting your performances to reflect your persistence and determination. When people watch you dance, what emotions or messages do you hope they take away?

JIHOON: When I practice alone in the studio, it’s usually very quiet. I genuinely enjoy that time and try to make it part of my everyday routine, though sometimes I wonder where all that effort is leading.

I think everyone is struggling with something in their own way. If someone who’s feeling exhausted by those struggles watches me dance, or even sees how I practice, I hope they can find a little strength in it.

There are so many incredible dancers who can move people through their technique alone. But if there’s something I want to offer through my own dancing, it’s encouragement. Even when I’m doing my best to shine onstage, behind it all, I’m just someone who’s working hard toward something, like everyone else.

If you could create a performance purely to express “Jihoon the artist,” what would it look like? What kind of movement or artistic direction would best represent who you are?

JIHOON: Just imagining it makes me happy. I’d love to create a video that really captures who I am as an artist. I don’t think there’s one particular style that defines me, and I consider my versatility one of my strengths. I’d want to bring together the things I love most and create something that makes me think, “This is me. This is something only I can do.”

More than convincing anyone else, I’d want to convince myself. On days when I lose confidence, I want to be able to watch that video and remind myself, “Right, I’m capable of this.” If I ever get the opportunity, that’s something I’d really love to accomplish.

You have a distinct artistic identity of your own. Within TWS, what aspect of “Kyungmin’s own color” are you most eager to develop and bring to the group’s music and performances?

KYUNGMIN: First of all, thank you for seeing me that way. I think my voice is one of the things I can contribute to the team, and I want to keep developing it so I can bring even more to TWS. Through my own vocal style, I hope to express both the playful and sophisticated sides of our music.

If you picture yourself five years from now, what kind of artist do you hope you’ll have become?

KYUNGMIN: I want to be an artist who never loses his ambition or sincerity. As you gain experience, things naturally become more familiar, and I think it’s easy to lose some of that drive. Even five years from now, I hope I’ll still be eager to try new things and challenge myself.

Sincerity matters just as much to me. As I grow older and gain more experience, I want to keep finding ways to move the fans who love us. Whatever form that takes, I hope I can continue giving them something that genuinely touches their hearts. Those are the two things I never want to lose.

This has been a pretty rough week for "Star Trek" royalty on this 60th anniversary year with the deaths of both Walter Koenig, "Star Trek's" Lt. Pavel Chekov on Sunday, Oct. 25 and Patrick Stewart, the storied sci-fi property's Captain Jean Luc-Picard on Wednesday, Oct. 28.

With the passing of Walter Koenig at the age of 90 this past week, franchise luminaries of all degrees are coming out with heartfelt condolences, kind words of remembrance, and tearful reflections.

William Shatner, 95, and George Takei, 89, represent the final remaining members of the U.S.S. Enterprise's core crew from "Star Trek: The Original Series" and they both took to social media to express their deep sorrow over losing one of their fellow travelers in the final frontier.

"I am deeply saddened to learn of Walter Koenig’s passing," Shatner posted on Instagram.

"Although we did not know each other well away from the set, we shared the later seasons of the original 'Star Trek' series and the six films that followed. What I observed, and what so many fans have expressed over the years, was a man who genuinely loved the 'Star Trek' community.

"At conventions, Walter was rarely content to remain behind a signing table. He preferred to be among the people who had kept 'Star Trek' alive for so many decades. That kind of genuine connection is rare, and it will be remembered by everyone who came into contact with him.

"My condolences to his family, his friends, and the countless fans whose lives he touched."

George Takei, who portrayed Lt. Hikaru Sulu and co-starred with Koenig on two seasons of "The Original Series" from 1967-69, as well as six subsequent "Star Trek" feature films, offered similar thoughts in memoriam.

"My heart is heavy. Walter Koenig, our Ensign Pavel Chekov, passed away early today," Takei shared on his Instagram page.

"Walter and I met on the bridge of the Enterprise in the 1960s, and we stayed friends for nearly six decades. When Brad and I married in 2008, Walter stood beside us as our best man. Just last month, on Sept. 14, he turned 90, on the same day Brad and I celebrated our 18th wedding anniversary. I will always treasure that he and I shared that date.

"Walter was more than Chekov. He was a writer, a teacher, a thoughtful man, and a loyal friend. To the fans who loved him for so many years, thank you. He loved you too.

"Rest well, my dear friend. Keep navigating a steady course."

Jeff Spry is an award-winning screenwriter and veteran freelance journalist covering TV, movies, video games, books, and comics. His work has appeared at SYFY Wire, Inverse, Collider, Bleeding Cool and elsewhere. Jeff lives in beautiful Bend, Oregon amid the ponderosa pines, classic muscle cars, a crypt of collector horror comics, and two loyal English Setters.

#723. With ‘The Girl of Your Dreams,’ Ashe Finds Her Sweet Spot: “I’m A Really Solid Version of Myself”

The pop singer's viral hit "Stop The Wedding!" continues to climb the Billboard Hot 100, reaching its highest peak yet this week with the top 25 in sight.

Ashe is tucked away in her Nashville home. It’s more of a cottage, she explains, a cup of coffee in hand. It’s straight out of The Holiday.

“It looks like a grandma decorated it,” the singer-songwriter tells The Hollywood Reporter on a recent Zoom call. “But it was in fact me.”

The 33-year-old is in the midst of a career-high. Her latest album, The Girl of Your Dreams, has earned the singer her highest Billboard 200 debut to date, landing at No. 20. The album’s pre-release single “Stop The Wedding!” has continued to climb the charts, landing at its highest-yet position at No. 28. Related Stories News Lenny Kravitz Debunks Viral Rumor That He Died in Horrific Learjet Plane Crash Music Marty Erlichman, Barbra Streisand's Longtime Manager, Dies at 97

It’s not the first time she’s experienced a viral moment — her 2019 single “Moral of the Story,” which was featured in Netflix’s To All The Boys I’ve Loved Before: P.S. I Still Love You, served as a breakout moment for the singer. Heading into the album, she was hopeful that the hype surrounding “Stop The Wedding!” would push people to listen to the entire album, which given its debut this week, it seems that came to fruition.

“‘Stop The Wedding!’ while to the world it stands alone and on its own little island, to me, it’s No. 1 of 11 songs,” she explains. “It lives in a body of work. I’m excited for people to have that context.”

There was a time for Ashe, whose real name is Ashlyn Rae Willson, when she felt extremely protective with her work. There’s always a complicated feeling when sharing an album with the world. But lately, thanks to her latest album and her 2025 stint as The Favors with collaborator Finneas, she’s finding herself moving away from that.

“A previous version of a previous songwriter that I was, was a bit more precious,” she says. “Now, as I’ve gotten older, it’s not that I wouldn’t take it less serious, but it’s art. It’s meant to be interpreted and perceived and misinterpreted.”

Adds Ashe: “I’m very OK with that — probably in a way that I didn’t used to be. I can’t wait for people who love it to love it. And for people that it’s not for, to not get it, and it just to be here.”

When did you notice something was happening with “Stop The Wedding!” and its rising viral moment?

I was on tour with Benson Boone when I started teasing “Stop The Wedding!” It came out while I was on that tour. I was able to feel the difference of that song pretty immediately. A couple days after it came out, I played it in L.A. and so much of the crowd of people who didn’t know who I was until now were singing the song. That was like, “OK, this feels different. Something about this is unique in its own thing.”

How are you processing it in relation to the album?

It’s a really singular, special song. I’d be devastated if I heard another artist put it out. If I heard that song and someone else put it out, I’d be like, “Whoa, no, that sounds like an Ashe song.” I’m really proud of its DNA. But it’s funny because while I have this true pride in it, I also have this distance from it now that it’s in the world and it’s becoming a part of people’s stories. It may mean more to someone who just left someone at the altar than it will ever mean to me. That’s bizarre and cool and awesome. This is the first time in my career that I have a healthy separation from the music. Not in a way that I don’t obsessively love it, but in a way that people’s reception of it is not a reflection on me and who I am and my worth as a person. I’ve never had that until now.

What do you think made the difference in finding yourself getting to that place?

Well, Nicole, I had a bit of a nervous breakdown in 2023, and I almost quit music, and it really took a lot of therapy and gardening and rediscovering why I really loved music and rediscovering that this is what I’m supposed to do. I am uniquely made to be a music artist. I’m uniquely made to be a songwriter. I feel uniquely equipped to handle this world, and I had to relearn that. I had to gain that confidence because I really lost the plot there for a second. Then put out my third record, Wilson, and then Finneas and I made The Dream. We made a whole ass band and put out a record. There was just so much healing and confidence that came from all of that, that now I’m a really solid version of myself.

I have so much to learn. Every day, there’s some new statistic with “Stop the Wedding!” My text thread with the label is like: “This new crazy thing just happened.” so I’m learning on the fly. This is a level of success that I have not had before, but I really know who I am, and I really like her. I love her. God forbid a girl like herself.

Do you think when you were starting out that you would’ve been equipped to handle the level of success you’re having now?

I do feel equipped to handle it now in a way that I definitely was not before. It’s funny, the universe, God, Oprah, whoever’s really in charge, I think [they] knew that this was a time that I could experience it and not lose myself to it. I don’t think that that would’ve have been the case in the past. It’s funny too, because I’ve been doing this for so long. There was so much I needed to learn and go through. You can see it from my first album to now, consistency has only just now clicked in. I think I really started to settle into my personal style and trusting my voice and what I have to say during The Favors album. That’s all been more recent as in the last three years.

It was right. It was correct that it happened this way. The real difference now is I so deeply love my life just as it is. I was deeply in love with my life before “Stop the Wedding!” came out. For all its extraordinary and very ordinary bits. “Stop the Wedding!” having this moment is not the point, it is the cherry [on top] to have a life that I’ve worked really hard for and to protect.

#721. Earth’s resources sustain humanity — but they come at a high price

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Richard Schiffman is an environmental journalist in New York City.

A huge lithium-mining operation in Chile’s Atacama Desert.Credit: AP Photo/Rodrigo Abd/Alamy

The Elements of Life: How Nitrogen, Phosphorus, and Potassium Nourish Us and Threaten the Planet Kerstin Hoppenhaus Greystone (2026)

The Vanishing Earth: Dispatches from the Frontiers of Extraction James Crawford Bloomsbury (2026)

For much of human history, our species has treated Earth as an inexhaustible source of raw materials. In the past half-century, people have taken more resources from the natural world than in our entire previous history. And the rate of extraction is rising as the global population grows.

Oil and gas drilling is shifting to the deep sea — here’s what is at stake

Oil and gas drilling is shifting to the deep sea — here’s what is at stake

Two books argue that we need to put the brakes on our unsustainable use of resources. In The Vanishing Earth, historian and journalist James Crawford recounts his travels to five landscapes that have been reshaped by drilling and mining.

And, in The Elements of Life, science journalist Kerstin Hoppenhaus examines the three elements vital for plant growth: nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium. Both books are informative and non-technical primers on humanity’s ever-increasing use of Earth’s dwindling resources.

Crawford developed an early interest in the impacts of mining as the son of a mechanical engineer who worked in extractive industries around the world, from the coal beds of Scotland to copper mines in Zambia and oil rigs in the North Sea. He is far from being the first to raise such concerns. First-century Roman naturalist Pliny the Elder wrote of how mining operations “urge us to our ruin” and wondered “when will be the end of thus exhausting the earth”.

Today’s industrial mining operations are on a scale Pliny could have hardly imagined, creating vast toxic areas called sacrifice zones that are, in some cases, uninhabitable. Crawford observed this at first hand when he visited the salt flats of the Atacama Desert in Chile, one of the world’s largest reserves of lithium. Lithium batteries are used in technologies from smartphones to electric vehicles, and demand for the element is expected to rise 50-fold by 2040, which would far outstrip our current ability to extract it.

How fertilizer shortages caused by the energy crisis threaten food security

How fertilizer shortages caused by the energy crisis threaten food security

In Chile, Crawford reports signs that the brine that is the source of lithium salts is already running out, threatening the wider ecosystem with collapse. Indigenous communities in the area are also finding that their water sources are drying up as mining activities deplete reserves stored in the underlying aquifer. The vast Salar de Atacama wetland, which is inhabited by three species of flamingo, might soon become a dead zone, unable to support aquatic life.

Some of the most common resources are also the most overexploited, the author contends. Global demand for clean water has doubled since 1960 and it is predicted that, by the middle of this century, nearly two-thirds of the world’s population will experience water stress, as intensive agriculture depletes aquifers and droughts become more frequent because of climate change. In cities, especially in arid areas, these problems can be exacerbated. Nearly all of China’s major cities are sinking because of subsidence resulting from aquifer depletion, and water shortages have imperilled cities from São Paulo in Brazil to Cape Town in South Africa. Such pressures have inspired schemes to tow icebergs from polar regions, but none has yet been implemented. Failure to tackle these issues could have catastrophic consequences. Struggles over water are projected to become a source of global conflict: water was once dubbed “the petroleum of the next century” in a report by the investment firm Goldman Sachs.

After water, sand is the world’s second most widely used resource. Crawford finds that it is also being over-extracted, as beaches worldwide are mined to meet the demand for construction concrete, which uses sand as its main ingredient. In Vietnam’s Mekong River Delta, intensive sand removal has caused whole sections of coastal farmland to collapse into the river and the ocean. Sand extraction in Sri Lanka has destroyed beaches, exacerbating the impact of sea-level rise and increasing the destructive power of the deadly 2004 tsunami. In India, illegal sand-mining operations have become so lucrative that they are a mainstay of organized crime.

The end of phosphate mining in Nauru has left behind a barren landscape of pinnacles.Credit: Auscape/UIG/Getty

Oil and other fossil fuels are unlikely to run out any time soon, but continued drilling poses a threat to biodiversity and human health. In the Ecuadorian jungle, for example, Crawford describes how chemicals released by drilling have caused cancer rates in the worst polluted areas to rise precipitously. In 2023, Ecuador became the first country where a citizen referendum voted to keep the oil in the ground, after previously becoming the first nation to grant legal rights to the natural world. Nevertheless, drilling continues for now in Ecuador, which, Crawford writes, has “tied its entire fate to oil”.

What can be done? Some environmental damage is inevitable when natural resources are extracted, but Crawford calls for a “repair revolution” to restore blighted landscapes. There is no such thing as “sustainable extraction”, he writes, but there must be “life … after extraction”.

#720. The Taurid meteor shower isn't much to look at. That's why I love it

The Taurids produce only a handful of meteors an hour. That sounds disappointing, but I've learned that expecting almost nothing can make this one of the most enjoyable meteor showers of the year.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I used to make a basic mistake with meteor showers — I treated the zenith hourly rate (ZHR) like a timetable. If a shower were advertised at 20 meteors per hour, I'd go outside expecting something roughly every three minutes. After 10 quiet minutes, I'd start wondering what I was doing wrong. After half an hour, I'd start to doubt the whole idea of meteor showers.

The Northern and Southern Taurids cured me of all that. Two linked meteor showers that peak around Nov. 4-5 and Nov. 11-12 this year, they each manage only about five meteors per hour under ideal conditions. In reality, you may see fewer. You may spend a long time seeing none. So what's the point?

I've come to regard their paucity of "shooting stars" as a feature, not a flaw, for the Taurids have taught me to stop counting meteors and instead just observe the sky. I go outside for Taurus, the Pleiades, Auriga, and whatever else happens to be visible. If a Taurid crosses the sky, excellent. If not, the evening hasn't failed. The reason is that they are also known for occasionally producing very bright meteors, or fireballs — although "occasionally" is important. Don't go outside expecting a procession of them.

The Taurids hit Earth's atmosphere at about 18 miles (29 kilometers) per second. That's relatively slow for a meteor shower. It's one reason Taurids can be more memorable than meteors from faster showers.

For observers across much of the Northern Hemisphere, Taurus rises in the east during the evening and becomes increasingly well placed as the night progresses. Later evening into the overnight hours is therefore the best time to watch.

I love looking at the night sky around Taurus, but you really don't need to stare at it if you're looking for Taurids. The radiant is indeed within Taurus (close to the Pleiades), but meteors can appear anywhere in the sky. Look roughly east or southeast, then watch as much sky as possible for an hour or so.

This year the moon helps out. The new moon falls on Nov. 9, leaving only a young waxing crescent around the shower's peak. It sets during the evening, giving us properly dark skies later on.

My Taurid observing strategy involves doing little direct meteor observing. I'll likely head outside once Taurus is reasonably high in the eastern sky, probably sometime in the later evening, and give myself other things to look at. The Pleiades are an obvious target — it's exciting to have this little open cluster back in the evening sky. So are the Hyades open cluster and bright orangey Aldebaran, also in Taurus. I'll probably set my smart telescope on the Pleiades and leave it alone to build up a long integration while I spend as much time as I can taking in the whole sky. Meteors are a naked-eye event and demand your attention — the second you avert your gaze from the night sky, a "shooting star" will appear. All stargazers know that!

I won't travel for hours to find perfect darkness. A darker location will reveal fainter meteors, for sure, but the Taurids' occasional bright members can be seen from less-than-perfect skies. A backyard is fine for this one — make travel plans only for August's Perseids and December's Geminids (moon phases allowing).

Nor will I keep score. Meteor rates are statistical descriptions, not promises. Five per hour does not mean one meteor every 12 minutes. You could see two close together and then nothing at all for hours. We're all so used to being told exactly what to expect, but the night sky doesn't work like that — you need to be open to whatever it throws at you (or not). Once you stop expecting the sky to do what you want, meteor showers become more enjoyable.

The moon is moving out of the early evening sky this week, which is exactly what stargazers wait for at this time of year. It reaches third quarter around Nov. 1, rising later at night and leaving the evening dark. That gives us a useful 10-night window for observing before moonlight becomes an issue.

I'm planning to use it for the Andromeda galaxy. From a genuinely dark location, M31 can be spotted with the naked eye as a faint patch. From brighter suburban skies, binoculars make life much easier. The beginner mistake is expecting anything resembling the photographs. Through binoculars, I'm looking for a subtle misty glow, not spiral arms. If you want a more impressive view, get yourself a smart telescope — they do a wonderful job on M31.

There's another practical change this weekend. Daylight saving time ends across most of the U.S. and Canada on Nov. 1. The stars haven't changed their schedule, of course, but getting outside under a dark sky after dinner — and even before — suddenly becomes much easier.

Although you don't need to stare at Taurus, the Bull, to see Taurids, it's an obvious target this week. It's climbing into the eastern sky during the evening. Bright orange star Aldebaran — a red giant 67 light-years from the solar system (and the most luminous star within 100 light-years) — marks the bull's eye. It appears to sit within a V-shape of stars that forms the bull's face. This is the Hyades, the closest open cluster of stars to the solar system at just 150 light-years.

The origin story of both Taurid meteor showers is genuinely awe-inspiring. They're associated with debris left in the inner solar system by Comet 2P/Encke, which orbits the sun once every 3.25 years (1,200 days) — the shortest orbital period of any known comet in the solar system, according to NASA. The second comet ever discovered, Encke, was discovered in 1786 and spans about 3 miles (4.8 kilometers) in diameter. It last reached perihelion — its closest point to the sun — on Oct. 22, 2023, and is due to do so again on Feb. 10, 2027, but Earth encounters debris associated with the comet every year.

The picture is more complicated than a single comet trail. The Southern and Northern Taurids are part of the broader Taurid Meteoroid Complex, a vast swarm of interplanetary dust, rocks, comets and asteroids thought to be related to Encke. It's thought that it originates from a much larger object that fragmented as it got close to the sun, perhaps just 5,000 to 6,000 years ago or as much as 20,000 years ago. Fears that huge, mile-wide "planet killer" asteroids may still reside in the Taurid Meteoroid Complex appear to have been ruled out. Phew.

Each fall, Earth passes through different parts of this sprawling stream, producing two overlapping meteor showers — and, occasionally, the larger fragments responsible for the Taurids' famous fireballs.

#719. ‘Dancing With the Stars’ Disney Night Makes Magic (3 Perfect Scores!) as Group Dances Return, Another Celeb Departs: See the Scores, Who Went Home

Cynthia Erivo joined as the night's special guest judge in a night meant to honor Disney stories and their stage adaptations.

[This story contains spoilers for episode nine of Dancing With the Stars season 35.]

It’s time for Disney Night on Dancing With the Stars.

This year’s Disney-themed episode sported a new Broadway twist, with “performances inspired by beloved Disney stories and their iconic stage adaptations,” per ABC. Couples paid homage to classics from Mary Poppins, The Little Mermaid, Tangled, Beauty and the Beast and many more.

Tuesday night’s episode also saw the return of the team dances, as co-hosts Alfonso Ribeiro and Julianne Hough each joined one of the group performances. Cynthia Erivo was also in the ballroom, joining as the night’s guest judge. Related Stories TV 'Dancing With the Stars' Disney Night Rescheduled Ahead of Midterms: When and Where to Watch Online 'Dancing' Diaries Ezra Frech on Tackling 'DWTS' Season 35 With Amber Glenn as "Teammates" and What Becoming the Show's First Amputee Winner Would Mean

Julia Stiles and Ezra Sosa were eliminated at the end of DWTS Disney Night. Earlier in the episode, they danced a paso doble to Hamilton‘s “Satisfied,” and were scored a 33/40.

Celebrities still competing on season 35 include Tatyana Ali, Jenna Dewan, Ezra Frech, Amber Glenn, Maura Higgins, Harry Shum Jr. and Connor Wood.

After the first dance of Disney Night, Hough announced that the couple who topped the leaderboard after the individual performances will receive immunity from next week’s dance-off. The couple who early on took that top spot was Harry and Jenna Johnson, who earned a perfect 40/40 for their jazz to “Supercalifragilisticexpialidocious” from Marry Poppins.

Harry and Jenna earned the first perfect score of DWTS season 35 last week, with Disney Night marking their second 40/40 in a row.

However, they weren’t left alone at the top of the Disney Night leaderboard for long, as Jenna and Val Chmerkovskiy also earned a 40/40 for their quickstep to Beauty and the Beast‘s “Be Our Guest.”

Because two couples tied at the top of the leaderboard, immunity for next week’s dance-off was given to the pair with the highest total of scores from across the season; Harry and Jenna toppled with a total of 236 (Jenna and Val had 235).

During last week’s Horror Movie Night, Jackson Olson and Tyler Cameron were kicked off the competition in a double elimination.

The couple with the lowest combined total of judges’ scores and viewer votes is eliminated at the end of each DWTS episode. Each viewer is allowed up to 10 votes per couple, per voting method (via ABC’s website and by text).

Live voting takes place during the East Coast airing of each show and ends shortly after the final performance; that means if you’re a West Coast viewer and want to vote, you must do so between 5 p.m. PT and roughly 6:45 p.m. PT, as voting ends after the final performance.

#718. Here’s Why the My Chemical Romance Lawsuit Really Ended, According to the Band’s Manager

Court filings reveal a new explanation for why the high-profile legal dispute with the Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders wrapped up so quickly.

My Chemical Romance had always planned to stop using Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders uniforms after just three concerts, and a headline-grabbing lawsuit from the cheer squad played no role in that decision, the band’s manager says in new court filings.

The cheerleaders sued last month, demanding a restraining order after the band’s backup dancers wore look-alike uniforms during shows at the Hollywood Bowl — the grand finale of a dystopian rock opera celebrating the 20th anniversary of the band’s The Black Parade album.

The case ended just days later, reportedly after My Chemical Romance promised not to use the costumes at future shows. But in a sworn statement filed in court Thursday (Oct. 29), the band’s manager, Brian Schechter, said that had always been the plan and was not a response to the lawsuit.

“From the outset, the Finale — with its elaborate sets, full cast, and resolution of the story told during the 2025 and 2026 tours — was planned to be performed only on Oct. 21, 23, and 24, 2026, and on no other date,” Schechter wrote in the Oct. 29 declaration.

“All of these decisions were made nearly a year before I first learned, on Oct. 22, 2026, after the Finale’s first performance, that [the cheerleaders] objected to it,” Schechter wrote. “The Finale was last performed on Oct. 24, 2026, because of those earlier decisions that it was the last performance of that three-part story, not because of any objection by plaintiff.”

In an emailed response to Billboard, Alex Spiro, lead counsel for the Cowboys Cheerleaders, flatly dismissed the idea that the band had already been planning to stop using the uniforms long in advance: “Sure they were,” he writes. “They waved the white flag.”

The band’s attorney did not immediately return a request for comment.

The Black Parade, the band’s 2006 magnum opus, reached the top of the Billboard 200 this week after an anniversary reissue. My Chemical Romance spent the past two years touring ahead of the looming milestone, culminating in the trio of theatrical concerts at the Hollywood Bowl last month. The shows, which told a satirical story about the “United States by Draag,” featured one scene in which the Cowboys Cheerleaders, armed with rifles, engaged in a faux-firefight on stage.

The cheerleaders’ parent company, Pro Silver Star, sued over that performance on Oct. 23, claiming the use of the look-alike uniforms infringed its trademark rights. Arguing fans and social media users had believed it was the real Cowboys Cheerleaders on stage, the case sought an immediate restraining order legally barring the band from using the uniforms at two final Bowl shows and any future dates.

Legal experts told Billboard the lawsuit faced long odds in court, since My Chemical Romance’s performance was likely protected by the First Amendment. But just days later, news broke that the band had agreed to not use the uniforms in future shows. TMZ, which broke the news based on anonymous sources, said the band had “folded” and that the cheerleaders had “won big.”

But in Thursday’s filing, Schechter said the lawsuit had nothing to do with the decision. He said the final two Hollywood Bowl shows had always been normal tour dates, not the elaborate “Finale” stage show — meaning the Cowboys cheer uniforms never would have appeared anyway. And he said there had never been a plan to use the costumes at other future dates.

“[In 2025], the band and I decided that the Finale would be performed only on the three original dates,” Schechter wrote in the declaration. “The Oct. 30 and 31, 2026, performances and the band’s remaining performances on its worldwide tour are not performances of the Finale and will not include any cheerleader characters or cheerleader costumes.”

The filing came with an attached exhibit, showing the actual email sent by the band’s lawyer (David Byrnes of the law firm Ziffren Brittenham LLP) the day before the news of the quick resolution broke.

“I write to let you know that there’s no need to proceed with the petition for a TRO attached to your email,” Byrnes wrote. “The Black Parade shows are finished and My Chemical Romance will not be performing any remaining shows on its current tour with dancers in the cheerleader costumes your client objects to.”

The new filings came during a brief moment last week when it appeared that Live Nation — the promoter of the Black Parade shows and thus a co-defendant in the cheerleader lawsuit — would continue to fight the case. The concert giant legally transferred the lawsuit to federal court, then filed a full brief arguing why the judge should refuse to grant the cheerleaders a restraining order.

“This is a trademark case about a musical group’s artistic expression and the First Amendment,” Live Nation’s lawyers write. “Plaintiff asks this court to use trademark law to line edit theatrical staging at a Los Angeles concert because plaintiff dislikes the way the show parodied one of the most famous uniforms in the United States.”

But on Monday morning (Nov. 2), that case ended, too, after the cheerleaders and Live Nation filed a joint motion telling the judge that they had reached an agreement for the “dismissal of this action, in its entirety.”

#717. ‘Red Before Dawn’ Review: A Road Movie Revisits the Indonesian Revolution in Ways More Didactic Than Climactic

Garin Nugroho’s wartime drama follows a group of disparate characters dangerously making their way across Indonesia as the fight for independence rages on.

Few people outside of Indonesia are likely to be familiar with the war of independence that began there just as WWII was coming to an end, resulting in hundreds of thousands of deaths at the hands of both Dutch soldiers and warring sectarian factions. The country finally achieved full emancipation from the Netherlands in 1949, though the wounds opened by the long and often brutal conflict would remain for the decades that followed.

Prolific Indonesian director Garin Nugroho revisits that pivotal historical period in Red Before Dawn (Merah Sebelum Fajar), a wartime road movie that condenses multiple aspects of the revolution into one rocky and dangerous trip through hostile territory. Following a cast of diverse characters who journey from Jakarta to Yogyakarta in 1946, facing countless obstacles but growing closer along the way, the film attempts to show how people from various ethnic and religious backgrounds managed to finally unite behind a single flag. Related Stories Business Tokyo: Industry Insiders Skeptical of Bold Japanese Government Plans for Overseas Content Sales Push Business Tokyo: Japan's New Production Incentives Risk Doing as Much Harm as Good Red Before Dawn The Bottom Line Historically intriguing but dramatically lacking. Venues: Tokyo International Film Festival Cast: Nicholas Saputra, Laura Basuki, Bront Palarae, Tissa Biani, Nagra Pakesadewo, Mariska SetiawanDirector, producer: Garin NugrohoScreenwriters: Garin Nugroho, Dirmawan Hatta 1 hour 53 minutes

On paper the idea is intriguing, and Red Before Dawn benefits from both an ambitious set-up and a highly cinematic setting, traveling through lush jungles and fields, rivers, villages and ancient ruins as the gang makes their way across the countryside in the year following Indonesia’s declaration of independence. Where the film falters is in its rather didactic brand of storytelling, with actors reciting reams of expository dialogue and situations that tend to feel more demonstrative than dramatic.

The pedagogical nature of the filmmaking is evident from the opening scene, which uses a theater piece to depict how the Dutch army showed zero mercy toward Indonesian freedom fighters during the war, labeling them as terrorists and executing them at will. (Estimates of casualties on the Indonesian side range from 100,000 to 250,000, with several million more displaced, versus roughly 15,000 dead on the Dutch side.) Animated sequences are also used to depict the inner thoughts of the film’s hero and narrator, Frans (Nicholas Saputra), a “half-blood” whose mixed Dutch and Indonesian heritage makes him a living, breathing example of the colonial battle that tore his country apart.

A respected engineer carrying a briefcase full of valuable geological surveys, Frans sets out on a mission to deliver his plans to the newly formed independent government that has set up shop in Yogyakarta, while other parts of Indonesia still remain under Dutch control. He enlists an Indian driver, Qasim (Bront Palarae), to steer their truck across deadly lands, bringing along a blind radio operator, Arya (Nagra Pakusadewo), who hopes to spread the revolutionary gospel over the airwaves. Along the way they also pick up a Chinese nurse, Fifi (Laura Basuki), and the lounge singer, Bandriah (Tissa Biani), making for an eclectic ensemble hailing from all walks of Indonesian life.

The 600-mile journey brings them face-to-face with hordes of their violent countrymen, whether it’s devout Muslims standing their ground, Chinese landowners facing persecution or a host of gun-toting rebels who see Frans and his crew as enemies rather than as fellow combatants. People get shot, stabbed, taken prisoner and kicked around, yet the tension is never high enough in a film that should be more thrilling. Music sequences, including a few songs performed by Biani, add some lightness to the proceedings, as does a romantic subplot between Frans and Fifi that winds up feeling superfluous.

Nugroho, a writer-director-producer who has nearly 40 movies under his belt in a career spanning over four decades, displays a solid level of craft throughout the adventure, especially in village settings that mix rural life with scenes of wartime devastation. But his narrative is ultimately more illustrative than organic, as if he needed to cover as many facets of the conflict as possible within a two-hour feature, not to mention explain the stakes to us over and over again, thus deflating much of the suspense.

Still, the traumas that Frans and the others face manage to leave their mark by the end of the journey, accumulating into a vision of the Indonesian revolution that underscores how violent the era truly was, yet how it was also filled with passion and hope among the people. True to its title, the film depicts the years before the dawn of a new nation as red ones indeed, marked by plenty of bloodshed but also a burning desire for freedom.

#715. The rocket scientist who summoned demons: The true horror story of Jack Parsons

Aside from helping lay the foundations for modern rocketry, Jack Parsons performed a bizarre series of ceremonies to try and conjure powerful supernatural entities.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In the winter of 1946, two men from very different walks of life walked into California's Mojave Desert together, where one of them became convinced an extraordinary experiment they had been conducting had finally succeeded.

One of the men was pioneering rocket scientist Jack Parsons, a self-taught chemist who helped establish what would become NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, and whose innovations in rocket propulsion would help lay the groundwork for the Space Race that would erupt in the years that followed. His unlikely companion was none other than L. Ron Hubbard, then a science fiction writer who had yet to compose the writings that would form the underpinnings of the Church of Scientology that he later established.

Despite Parsons' work with rockets and his companion Hubbard's fictional writings about them, their work together in the early months of 1946 had nothing to do with rocket propulsion, spacecraft, or other technological innovations that would eventually carry humans to space. Instead, Parsons and Hubbard were engaged in an elaborate series of occult ceremonies at the time, whereby they intended to summon an elemental feminine goddess known as "Babalon" (not to be confused with Babylon) to help them bring an otherworldly entity into physical existence.

Their efforts, known today as the "Babalon Working," represent one of the most unusual affairs in American history, with tangential connections to the history of space exploration.

Given its strangeness, the episode has garnered attention from several scholars and historians over the decades, who have sought to understand a series of events at the intersection of science and the occult involving one of the most unconventional innovators behind modern rocket propulsion.

Parsons, born in 1914, would become a key figure in the early development of American rocket technologies by the 1930s and 1940s in California, ultimately helping establish what would become the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL). His contributions included the historic experiments at Pasadena's Arroyo Seco on Halloween Day in 1936, which NASA now recognizes as the foundational experiments that launched JPL.

Very much in contrast with his scientific aptitudes, Parsons also cultivated an interest in ceremonial magic during this period. By the early 1940s, he had immersed himself within the California chapter of the Ordo Templi Orientis (OTO), the organization associated with the infamous British occultist Aleister Crowley and his religious philosophy known as Thelema. In 1943, Parsons became the new leader of the organization's Agape Lodge, which subsequently began operating out of his Pasadena residence on South Orange Grove Avenue.

Parsons' occult interests became particularly focused on the evocation of supernatural entities during this period, which the young rocket scientist seemed to genuinely believe could be manifested in the physical world through ritual practices. Ultimately, this led him to undertake an ambitious — and utterly bizarre — series of ceremonies aimed at conjuring what was supposedly one of Thelema's most powerful supernatural entities.

Parsons first became acquainted with L. Ron Hubbard in the summer of 1945, and shortly after meeting, Hubbard became a resident of the scientist's Pasadena home.

While Hubbard had no formal training in the occult arts, Parsons felt he demonstrated the kinds of aptitudes that would make him a promising partner for a serious ceremonial magic undertaking. Thus, in the first days of January 1946, the pair embarked on a series of rituals, which Parsons documented in a manuscript that later became known as The Book of Babalon.

"In the introduction to this text [Parsons] explained that the underlying philosophy for the Babalon Working is that the present age is under the influence of a violent force," noted University of Gothenburg scholar Henrik Bogdan in a 2016 article published in the journal Numen. "The invocation of Babalon was thus, according to Parsons, an attempt to prevent the world from being destroyed."

Specifically, Parsons believed the force of Babalon could be manifested in a specific woman. "In this sense, the Babalon Working was not only an exercise in ritual magic, but a deliberate attempt to bring a divine feminine force into human form," Bogdan notes. With this goal in mind, during the first two weeks of January 1946, the pair worked to invoke this divine feminine figure, associated with liberation and spiritual transformation according to Crowley's Thelemic system.

On January 18, 1946, Parsons and Hubbard traveled into the Mojave Desert, where, according to Parsons' later writings, a change in atmosphere involving their ritual work suddenly became apparent. Now believing their operation had been a success, Parsons declared their work completed, and the two returned to Pasadena.

Soon afterward, Parsons reported to Hubbard that his elemental mistress had seemingly manifested with the sudden appearance at his home of a blue-eyed, red-haired artist named Marjorie Elizabeth Cameron. A former member of the U.S. Navy's WAVES program, Cameron had been invited to Parsons' residence by a colleague who, like Hubbard, was also lodging there at the time. Upon seeing her, Parsons became convinced this was the elemental lover he and Hubbard had worked to conjure, thereby confirming that the Babalon Working had produced its intended result.

Soon, Parsons and Cameron began a relationship, and borrowing ideas from Crowley's 1929 novel Moonchild, Parsons now believed that his romance with Cameron could facilitate the incarnation of a supernatural force through the literal conception of a child using ritual sex magic. The result, Parsons believed, could help to bring about a transformative new dawn in humanity's spiritual development.

This phase of the Babalon Working mainly involved magic rituals and Enochian incantations performed by Parsons and Cameron, with Hubbard present and assisting (in addition to having proposed Rachmaninoff's "Isle of the Dead" as an eerie sonic backdrop for the occasion). For Parsons, the ultimate goal had been to conceive a "magical child" that would become the newborn Thelemic messiah.

Following completion of the rituals in late February 1946, Cameron left on a trip to New York, and Parsons returned to the Mojave Desert where he completed a short treatise entitled Liber 49, believing it to be a "channeled" fourth and final portion of The Book of the Law, Crowley's foundational Thelemic text.

Upon returning from New York, Cameron even claimed to have observed an unusual aerial object—something akin to what later became known as "flying saucers" in the summer of the following year—which she believed to represent the "war engine" referenced in Crowley's work.

Crowley, however, was considerably less enthusiastic about all this. Upon learning what Parsons, Hubbard, and Cameron had been involved with, the famed British occultist confided to a colleague in an April 1946 correspondence that "Apparently he [Parsons] or Ron or somebody is producing a Moonchild. I get fairly frantic when I contemplate the idiocy of these louts."

Ultimately, a growing divide between Crowley and Parsons would cost the rocket scientist his leadership of the Agape Lodge, prompting his departure from Crowley's OTO before the end of 1946. His relationship with Hubbard similarly dissolved due to Parsons' worsening financial situation. Nevertheless, Parsons soldiered on, marrying Cameron in October 1946 and continuing his efforts to usher in a new spiritual age.

On June 17, 1952, Parsons' unusual life ended prematurely when an explosion occurred in his home laboratory, resulting in fatal injuries. He was only 37 years old. Questions still surround the circumstances of his death; while it was ruled an accident, there have been allegations that it was suicide or even a murder.

During his short life, Parsons still managed to make significant contributions to the science of rocket propulsion, securing a place in the history of American space exploration — albeit one that is often overshadowed by the interest historians and scholars have taken in his occult activities.

Nonetheless, Parsons remains a key figure responsible for helping lay the early foundations for what would become America's space program. Although decades before NASA would begin sending its spacecraft in pursuit of answers to cosmic mysteries, one of its early technological pioneers had been seeking answers to such cosmic questions in a very different way: by exploring the boundary between our physical world and the supernatural realms beyond.

Anthony Testa, The Key of the Abyss: Jack Parsons, the Babalon Working and the Black Pilgrimage Decoded (2006), p. 128.

"Babalon Working." Occult Wiki. Accessed Oct. 29, 2026.

Bogdan, Henrik. "The Babalon Working 1946: L. Ron Hubbard, John Whiteside Parsons, and the Practice of Enochian Magic." Numen, Vol. 63, No. 1, 2016, pp. 12–32.

Carter, John. Sex and Rockets: The Occult World of Jack Parsons. New edition. Feral House, 2004.

Josephson Storm, Jason Ānanda. "Sex, Magic, & Rockets or the Implications of the Babalon Working for Theories of Belief and Rationality." Method & Theory in the Study of Religion, Vol. 37, 2025, pp. 323–335.
